title: Nachni: The Saga of Art Unappreciated
abstract: The Nachni s of Purulia are a group of women dancers who dance to the characteristic Jhumur of rural Bengal. The dance form of the Nachni is without a doubt part of the cultural heritage of Bengal—and in a broader sense, of India. Yet, a closer look at the community would show up a distinctive lack of acknowledgement about this art form. On the contrary, these women, these dancers are most of the time stigmatized and looked down upon, so much so that these women themselves have come to see their profession as something not to be proud of. This paper proposes to talk of the Nachni s in the Rarh Bengal area—especially, Purulia—to unearth some not-so-pretty causes for the stigma that keeps these artisans of Nachni dance from holding their head high in society.

title: Cultural Emotion Recognition: Detecting Navarasa in Indian Classical Dance with CNNs
abstract: One of the initial ideas in the Indian classical aesthetics, the Navarasa, sums up nine different emotions: Shringara (love), Hasya (joy), Karuna (sorrow), Raudra (anger), Veera (courage), Bhayanaka (fear), Bibhatsa (disgust), Adbhuta (wonder), and Shanta (tranquility). The ability to recognize these expressions based on the facial expressions is crucial to maintaining cultural heritage, and also in the advancement of performing arts training, as well as allowing advanced human-computer interaction. In this paper, a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based scheme of automated Navarasa detection on Indian classical dance performances is introduced. A personal dataset was created in partnership with dance schools that included 350 images per emotion category created using the methods of data augmentation, including rotation, flipping, scaling, and lighting changes. Preprocessing of images was done through conversion to grayscale, removing noise, and increasing edges and then normalization. The CNN architecture proposed combines the convolutional and max-pooling layers, ReLU activation, and fully connected layers to make the classification. The model produced an accuracy of 94.12, but the majority of classes of emotions are above 92 in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score. The proposed model demonstrates a high level of generalization in the cultural sphere, despite the fact that the data has been gathered in relatively controlled settings, which, in turn, might reduce diversity. The proposed approach has higher accuracy when compared to recent FER methods, a standard CNN model with an accuracy of 71.61% on FER- 2013, a hybrid LBP CNN model with an accuracy of 90.20% on CK +, and a lightweight CNN model with an accuracy of 91% on CK +. These findings highlight the effectiveness of deep learning in cultural emotion recognition, and that deep learning can be used in practice in automated feedback when teaching performing arts, emotion-sensitive interactive systems, and digital cultural heritage projects.

abstract: This paper explores how India employs cultural diplomacy and diaspora politics as major components of its soft power strategy in contemporary international relations. Drawing upon soft power theory, the study examines how India’s cultural heritage, democratic identity, and global diaspora networks contribute to its international influence. Through initiatives such as global yoga promotion, educational exchanges, cultural festivals, and structured diaspora engagement platforms, India seeks to enhance its global image and strategic partnerships. The paper argues that cultural appeal combined with diaspora engagement creates a sustainable framework for influence beyond military or economic means. However, effective coordination and credibility remain essential for long-term impact.

title: IMPROVING COGNITIVE SKILLS VIA THE TRADITIONAL DANCE PEDAGOGY OF KERALA: A NOVEL APPROACH FOR CHILDREN WITH LEARNING DISABILITIES
abstract: Improving cognitive skills through the traditional dance pedagogy of Kerala presents a novel and promising approach for children with learning disabilities. This method leverages the rich cultural heritage of Kerala's classical dance forms, such as Kathakali and Mohiniyattam, integrating their intricate movements, rhythmic patterns, and expressive techniques into therapeutic and educational settings. The structured and repetitive nature of these dances aids in enhancing memory, attention, and coordination, while the storytelling aspect fosters language development and social skills. By creating an engaging and multisensory learning environment, traditional dance pedagogy not only supports cognitive development but also boosts self-esteem and emotional well-being, offering a holistic and culturally resonant intervention for children with learning disabilities.

title: Natural Rights Theory of Copyright Protection
abstract: Copyright protection is above all one of the means of promoting, enriching and disseminating the national cultural heritage. A country's development depends to a very great extent on the creativity of its people, and encouragement of individual creativity and its dissemination is a sine qua non for progress. Copyright constitutes an essential element in the development process. Experience has shown that the enrichment of the national cultural heritage depends directly on the level of protection afforded to literary and artistic works. The greater the number of a country‟s intellectual creations, the higher its renown; the greater the number of productions in literature and the arts, the more numerous their so-called “auxiliaries” (the performers, producers of phonograms and broadcasting organizations) in the book, record and entertainment industries; and indeed, in the final analysis, encouragement of intellectual creation is one of the basic prerequisites of all social, economic and cultural development. Copyright protection, from the viewpoint of the creator of works, makes sense only if the creator actually derives benefits from such works, and this cannot happen in the absence of publication and dissemination of his works and the facilitation of such publication and dissemination. This is the essential role of copyright in developing countries. As far as natural right theorists are concerned they move on the North Pole and egalitarians on the South Pole vis-a-vis property right is concerned. Especially Robert Nozick and Marx appear radically opposite to each other. One is advocating exclusive property right without any intervention even from the state. And other is advocating for no private property. Both conception is disastrous for society at large. In between, one of the greatest philosophers of 20th century Prof. John Rawls comes into rescue. He advocates for „justice as fairness.‟ He creates a hypothetical condition; an original position wherein people are ignorant about themselves. There is a veil of ignorance while people participating in social contract have to choose certain principles to ensure justice.

title: Assessing ‘Mata Bhavani Stepwell, Asarwa, Ahmedabad’ as a Case of Living Heritage
abstract: There is abundance of culture and heritage in Ahmedabad, which holds a rich array of meaning and significance. Water structures had a great significance in the historical era particularly in and around the western zone of India. Over the period of time their importance has been gradually decreasing and few of them have been totally neglected as well. On the other hand, there have been communities who religiously believe in some structures. These people have tried to keep the heritage site active. One such approach which has come to light latterly is the ‘Living Heritage Approach’. In 2003, a new term, ‘Living Heritage’ was coined by UNESCO in order to conserve the heritage sites. This approach has served to keep the community connections intact, thereby keeping the site functional. Presently, some of the water structures particularly stepwells are being taken care or are in use, not for primary use but for various other purposes. The change in purpose has resulted in modifications and alterations to historical structures. Therefore, there is a need to conserve these heritage marvels of our past for future generations. The research aims to assess the values and characteristics of living heritage in the Mata Bhavani stepwell. The particular stepwell is selected because it is still functional and the beliefs of the community are attached to it. This research articulates the tangible and intangible attributes, derived from various literature reviews. The living heritage approach of Ioannis Poulios and UNESCO is used as a base which is altered to some extent in order to assess the case of Mata Bhavani Stepwell. The study looks into three major values - Historical, Social and Cultural. This research serves as a lens for evaluating the ‘Living Heritage Approach’ for similar sites.

title: Preservation of Textual Heritage With Stress to Malayalam Manuscripts
abstract: India has a vast cultural heritage. One of the main categories of it is textual heritage. Heritage conservation activities to protect textual heritage available in various forms such as palm leaves and paper from destruction are the necessity of the times. Digitization is one of the most important processes in textual heritage conservation. Although millions of texts have been preserved in this way, the process faces various challenges. The best method available today to solve them is to prepare XML from the Unicode source of the text and then store the text in various formats such as HTML, ePub, and MediaWiki. It is essential to consider the content and layout of the text as different entities and to understand the importance of the text in it and move towards innovative text-centric conservation methods. “Sayahna” is presented as a good example of such a method in Malayalam.

title: The Cultural Politics of Storytelling inTree Matters(2014) by Gangu Bai
abstract: The paper attempts to read the children’s picturebook Tree Matters (2014) by Gangu Bai, a Bhil artist, and published by Tara Books, to understand how the cultural politics of storytelling in the book works to underline the complex structure of social injustice and exclusion at play in the right and access to the forest in the case of the Bhil tribe in India. The relationship of the Bhil women with the forest is multidimensional, and the art and narrative by Gangu Bai in the picturebook represents this. The paper argues that the cultural politics of storytelling practiced by the artist reiterates this special relationship with the trees in the forest, and at the same time also makes use of this relationship to assert the unique cultural heritage and identity of the community. The subversive nature of children's books that creatively introduces complex issues of social injustice and environmental politics is also explored.

abstract: This chapter analyzes the current situation of research within Cambodia's higher education system, emphasizing the obstacles faced, including insufficient funding, limited research facilities, and a deficiency of suitably trained researchers. title: A Study on the Factors Contributing to Tourism Attractiveness of Kashmir Valley
abstract: This study investigates the factors contributing to the tourism attractiveness of Jammu and Kashmir and their influence on tourist behavior and attitudes. By analyzing key destination attributes such as natural beauty, cultural heritage, hospitality, infrastructure, and amenities, the research examines how these factors shape tourists' satisfaction, intention to revisit, and likelihood of recommending the destination. A structured questionnaire was designed and validated through expert feedback and a pilot test, followed by data collection from 370 valid respondents. The findings reveal that scenic landscapes, cultural experiences, and hospitality significantly enhance tourist attitudes, which in turn drive positive behavioral intentions. The study also explores the moderating effects of demographic variables, offering valuable insights for stakeholders to enhance destination appeal and improve tourist experiences.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE HUMANITIES: EMERGING PERSPECTIVES AND INTERDISCIPLINARY POSSIBILITIES
abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence has significantly transformed various fields of knowledge, extending its influence beyond science and technology into the domain of the humanities. Traditionally associated with human creativity, interpretation, and critical thought, the humanities are now engaging with AI as both a methodological tool and a subject of inquiry. This paper examines the role of Artificial Intelligence in the humanities by exploring its applications in literary studies, history, linguistics, philosophy, and cultural analysis. It highlights how AI-driven tools enable new forms of research, reinterpretation of texts, and preservation of cultural heritage while also raising ethical, philosophical, and epistemological concerns. The study argues that AI does not replace humanistic inquiry but reshapes it by offering innovative approaches that expand the scope of humanities scholarship.

title: The Role of Temple Sculptures in Narrating Mythology and Cultural History
abstract: Temple sculptures serve not merely as decorative adornments of sacred architecture but as a profound medium for visual storytelling narrating mythology, encoding cosmological symbolism, and reflecting social and cultural history. Through carefully carved deities, mythic narratives, celestial beings, dancers, everyday life scenes, and symbolic motifs, sculptures transform a temple into a three-dimensional text that communicates religious beliefs, moral values, cosmic order, and societal life across generations. These sculptural narratives help preserve collective memory, transmit cultural heritage, reinforce religious identities, and offer insights into socio-economic, artistic, and spiritual milieus of their times. In this way, temple sculpture becomes both a spiritual bridge between the human and divine and a historical record of the civilization that created it.

title: DECLINING TRADITIONAL OCCUPATIONS IN KARNATAKA – A HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE
abstract: This paper examines the gradual decline of traditional occupations in Karnataka from a historical perspective. It explores how pre-colonial economic systems, colonial interventions, and post-independence modernization have contributed to the weakening of hereditary occupations such as weaving, pottery, leatherwork, folk performance, agriculture-based crafts, and nomadic services. The study highlights how industrialization, changing market demands, and urbanization have disrupted community-based livelihoods. It also analyzes the socio-economic consequences of occupational decline, including unemployment, migration, and loss of indigenous knowledge systems. The paper concludes that while modernization has created new opportunities, it has also endangered cultural heritage and traditional skills that once formed the backbone of Karnataka’s rural economy

title: THE FUTURE OF CONSTRUCTION IN INDIA: EMBRACING PREFABRICATION
abstract: Prefabrication technology involves the off-site production of building components for on-site assembly, offers significant potential benefits for developing nations such as China, India, Africa, and many regions of South America. This technology promises to enable the rapid and cost-effective construction of homes, addressing acute housing shortages driven by rapid urbanisation and population growth. However, the widespread adoption of prefabrication poses challenges particularly concerning the preservation of cultural heritage, the fostering of community cohesion, and the reliance on a limited number of skilled workers. This paper uses India as a case study to examine the benefits and drawbacks of prefabrication in this context and provides recommendations for how architects from affluent nations and regional building experts can integrate cultural and technological considerations to promote sustainable development.

title: WOOL, WORSHIP, AND WEFT: CULTURAL SEMIOTICS IN THE DHABHLA WEAVE OF KUTCH
abstract: The Dhabhla weave of Kutch, Gujarat, is recognized as a lesser-known woolen textile tradition, deeply rooted in spiritual, symbolic, and cultural significance. Traditionally created by the Vankar weaving communities and used by the Rabari pastoralists, these textiles are valued not just for their utility but for the layered meanings woven into their motifs, colors, and ritual applications. This study investigates the semiotic dimensions of the Dhabhla weave through ethnographic fieldwork and visual-textile analysis. It focuses on how these embedded symbols are understood by both weavers and users, how their meanings have transformed over time, and what these shifts suggest for the preservation of intangible cultural heritage. With evolving markets and the rise of contemporary design collaborations, the research also considers the effects of cultural translation, design intervention, and the potential dilution of symbolic content

title: Heritage entrepreneurship: Cultural and creative pursuits in business management. By VanessaRatten (Ed.), Palgrave Studies in Global Entrepreneurship. ISBN 978‐981‐19‐5148‐0, ISBN 978‐981‐19‐5149‐7 (eBook), https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-19-5149-7
abstract: Research in Entrepreneurship and innovation has witnessed growing interest from entrepreneurial scholars and academia across the globe (Carlsson et al., 2013). Value addition to products and services has been proposed as a key strategy for entrepreneurs. Heritage holds one such intrinsic value which if incorporated into a product or service can significantly enhance its utility. This provides a novel opportunity for entrepreneurs to leverage heritage in their business models to make them more socially sound and resilient. Heritage carries different worth for different people and hence the definitions vary accordingly. But the common social and cultural thread that ties generations over time has always existed and evolved. Be it tangible architectural monuments or intangible folklore and stories, they hold a special place in the heart of the people in the region. With increasing disposable income among the people, the propensity to seek and value heritage commodities has also increased (Chhabra et al., 2003). This holds immense potential for entrepreneurship and its stakeholders to integrate cognitive and cultural components to its products, services, and strategies to magnify the overall appeal. This needs a paradigm shift in how we accommodate heritage in the business sphere and warrants focused attention from the industry and academia to explore newer possibilities, channels, and strategies to realize its true potential. The research in entrepreneurship and its sub-domains have used the same theories over time (Newman et al., 2019). A more refined theory for heritage entrepreneurship brings possibilities of more precision and accuracy in the findings of heritage entrepreneurial research. This will both help academia and the industry with a clear and better view and benchmark to measure their progress. Social and community entrepreneurship subdomains do bear resemblance to heritage entrepreneurship, but the legacy of the past is what sets heritage entrepreneurship apart and makes it more special. This new attribute calls for special attention of researchers towards its business value. Against this backdrop, the book Heritage Entrepreneurship: Cultural and Creative Pursuits in Business Management, sets the tone for the academic inquiry and business pursuits of heritage entrepreneurship by academia and entrepreneurs respectively. It calls for incorporating heritage aspects within entrepreneurial business ventures. The book has nine chapters with Chapter 1 clearly and comprehensively defining and delineating heritage entrepreneurship and its attributes. The chapter combines elements from entrepreneurship with cultural and tourism theories to constitute a novel heritage entrepreneurship theory and establish it as the youngest field of entrepreneurship research. While calling Heritage entrepreneurship a subdomain of cultural entrepreneurship, it also subtly differentiates heritage entrepreneurship from cultural or tourism entrepreneurship through its special emphasis on history. The chapter further describes the different types of heritage and heritage tourists and talks about World heritage site (WHS) branding and their sustainability. Chapter 2 talks about how government can act as an enabler in catalyzing the growth of community-based entrepreneurial ecosystems. It presents a case of a government scheme in Thailand to show that it is not always the case that the absence of government efforts is what gives birth to social enterprises. Rather the government and public agencies can act proactively to promote social and cultural entrepreneurship. Chapter 3 examines the antecedents of social innovation and investigates how local and social attributes like trust and support can act as drivers of social innovation through greater coordination and cooperation of the community stakeholders. The knowledge-based theory of firms is used in Chapter 4 to investigate the innovation strategies used by family businesses during succession. It uses a qualitative approach to investigate 18 family businesses in Indonesia and has discovered four ways that family businesses can innovate during the succession process: defending strategy, postponing strategy, ad-hoc strategy, and systematic strategy. It also sheds light on how succession causes tradition versus innovation tensions and how different actors use segregation, reinterpretation, and recombination strategy to successfully manage those tensions. Chapter 5 conducts a bibliometric analysis to explore relationships between informal entrepreneurship and heritage entrepreneurship. Along with establishing the literary and publication facts relating to the field of informal and heritage entrepreneurship, it also investigates important issues like the progression of research in the field of gender diversity and its implications for business performance. Chapter 6 discusses how the pandemic has brought a shift in tourist preferences in the Swiss Alps and highlights the gaps in service innovation. The arrival and stay patterns have changed from longer stays to more frequent short stays. The choice of transport and stay has also witnessed a shift from public to private and from hotels to serviced apartments and campsites due to sanitary reasons. The blurring of boundaries between home and workplace further magnifies these shifts. To cater to these changes, it calls for the development of multilocal living and new service development as an iterative process following a customer-centric logic. The major World Heritage Sites (WHS) in Italy and the United States are highlighted in Chapters 7 and 8, respectively. It outlines their cultural relevance and the value of cultural tourism for regions' economic and social advancement. It also looks at how WHS encourages tourism growth based on a person's interest in history. Chapter 9 proposes a new model of Heritage entrepreneurship and establishes the future trends in the field. The model describes the influencing factors, challenges, and outcomes of heritage entrepreneurship. It also lays down future research paths focused on measuring the value of heritage entrepreneurship using stakeholders' perspectives and how collaboration can be a key enabler in promoting heritage entrepreneurship ecosystems. The chapter outlines multidisciplinary research avenues using economics, finance, social and entrepreneurial lenses to investigate this domain to bring up concrete evidence in various listed streams and sub-streams. The book beautifully brings to the surface the potential value underlying the heritage and establishes an entrepreneurial approach to leverage it. This opens opportunities for unlocking the economic value of heritage which can go a long way in promoting the economic development and sustainability of regions through the growth of heritage-focused businesses. Entrepreneurs, communities, governments, and other stakeholders can take a leaf out of this book which can help them in creating significant economic and social value. Technology has been at the heart of entrepreneurship in recent times (Muñoz et al., 2016). The book emphasizes economic, financial, and social aspects but lacks the technology angle as to how and what role technology can play in heritage entrepreneurship. The book calls for value creation using heritage and outlines future research opportunities in creating and measuring value. But making heritage a commodity has huge ramifications for society, the community, and ecology. This side of the research landscape is not so clearly promoted which is needed to balance economic development with sustainability. The book Heritage “Entrepreneurship: Cultural and Creative Pursuits in Business Management” firmly establishes heritage entrepreneurship as a separate field of research. Entrepreneurial research scholars can find this book as a one-step guide to a novel research area holding immense potential. The definitions, classifications, and future research themes and suggestions provide a ready-made recipe for productive research output. This will further the purpose of the book through the creation and validation of new heritage entrepreneurship theories enriching the field of entrepreneurship and its domains. Deepak Kumar is a joint PhD student from the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur, India, and Latrobe University, Australia. His research area includes small businesses and entrepreneurship, Finance, and Blockchain. He has done his bachelor's in Information Technology and MBA in finance from ABV-IIITM Gwalior India.

title: Romans through the lens of their architecture
abstract: The Roman Empire is one of history’s most prominent, wealthiest, and influential civilisations. Spreading over much of Europe, Western Asia and North Africa, the Romans ruled the Mediterranean. Lasting many years, the empire went through social, political and economic external and internal developments, with each emperor and later senators that replaced their predecessors implementing different policies, campaigns and actions. This left the empire in a constant revolutionary state until its eventual downfall due to civil unrest and barbarian invasion. However, its architecture and monuments symbolise consistency and its legacy within the empire. The architecture of ancient Rome provides valuable insights into various aspects of Roman society, helping us gain a deeper understanding of its structure and changes over time. By examining these architectural elements, we can better comprehend the complexities of Roman life and culture. Roman architecture featured arches, domes, columns, and, most importantly, designs and sculptures alluding to Roman society's social, political, economic or religious aspects. Buildings were constructed for pagan gods, and later, churches were built. They served as monuments for military triumphs and were designed to depict power and strength, among other factors. Consequently, understanding their architecture provides deeper insights into Roman cultural identity. Cultural identity refers to a sense of belonging to a particular group, which may result from an overlap of social, economic, and cultural beliefs and values. This essay will explore how the Roman architecture and monuments, especially temples, arches and entertainment structures, reflect and present the cultural identity of the empire. This will be done through a literary analysis of the three most prominent monuments of the Roman empire: The Arch of Constantine, The Colosseum , and The Pantheon.

title: Assessing the Economic Impact of Homestay Tourism in Rural Communities
abstract: Homestay tourism in rural communities offers an immersive travel experience, fostering cultural exchange and driving economic growth in underserved areas. This study assesses its economic impact by examining income generation, job creation, and local business development. Direct expenditures on accommodations, food, and services stimulate rural economies and reduce poverty. Additionally, homestay tourism promotes sustainable community involvement through partnerships between residents and local governments, enhancing infrastructure and preserving cultural heritage. However, challenges such as income inequality, seasonality, and environmental impacts require balanced management. This research provides a holistic analysis of homestay tourism's contributions and challenges, emphasizing its role as a vital tool for rural development and economic diversification.

title: Overtourism in India Challenges, Impacts and Sustainable Solutions: A Case Study of Kumbh Mela
abstract: Overtourism in India has emerged as a significant challenge due to rapidly increasing visitor numbers placing immense pressure on natural, cultural, and infrastructural resources. While tourism provides important economic benefits including employment and foreign exchange, its negative impacts are becoming more pronounced: environmental degradation, overcrowding, infrastructural strain, and loss of cultural authenticity. Iconic destinations such as the Taj Mahal, Goa, and Varanasi face threats from unsustainable tourism practices. Using a case study of the Kumbh Mela, this paper examines the causes and consequences of overtourism in India. It evaluates environmental, social, cultural, and economic impacts, reviews current government / stakeholder initiatives, and proposes sustainable solutions to balance tourism growth with preservation of cultural heritage and environmental integrity.

title: The History of Archery
abstract: This article analyzes the history of the emergence of the sport of archery, its role in the development of mankind, and the stages of its formation as a sport. The study highlights the fact that the bow and arrow were initially used as a means of hunting and protection in primitive society, and later became a means of military training and competition. It also provides information on the development of archery in the history of the peoples of the East and West, its role in ancient civilizations, and its international popularity as a sport. The article analyzes the formation of modern archery, the activities of international sports organizations, its inclusion in the Olympic Games, and the stages of development of this sport in Uzbekistan. The results of the study show that archery is not only a historical and cultural heritage, but also an important sport in the physical, spiritual, and volitional education of young people.

title: Tribal Contributions to Indian Culture: A Special Reference to Maharashtra
abstract: India’s cultural identity has been significantly shaped by its tribal communities, who constitute nearly 8.6% of the national population. Maharashtra, home to diverse tribes such as the Warli, Bhil, Gond, Katkari, Korku, and Thakar, presents a unique cultural mosaic that blends art, music, rituals, and ecological wisdom. Tribal contributions are visible in globally recognized art forms like Warli paintings, indigenous agricultural practices such as millet cultivation, vibrant folk dances, and nature-based festivals. This paper explores these contributions with special reference to Maharashtra, emphasizing their enduring impact on Indian cultural heritage. The study also highlights the challenges faced in preserving tribal traditions in the modern era, while underlining the need for documentation, policy support, and cultural promotion.

title: GENERIC LOSSLESS VISIBLE WATERMARKING BY USING TRANSLUCENT AND MONOCHROME METHOD
abstract: Images make up a major component of multimedia content. Digital arts, illustrative diagrams, cultural heritage paintings in digitized for and digital photographs are examples of images. Advances in computing hardware, software, and computer networks have created threats to copyright protection and content integrity. In this paper, a new method for lossless visible watermarking is proposed by using appropriate compound mappings that allow mapped values to be controllable. The mappings are proved to be reversible for lossless recovery of the original image. The approach is generic, leading to the possibility of embedding different types of visible watermarks into cover images. Two applications of the proposed method are demonstrated, where opaque monochrome watermarks and non uniformly translucent full-color ones are respectively embedded into color images.

title: RHYTHM, MOVEMENT AND MARGINALITY : A STUDY OF KALBELIYA FOLK DANCE
abstract: Kalbeliya folk dance, originating from the Kalbeliya community of Rajasthan, represents a vibrant synthesis of rhythm, movement, and cultural identity. Traditionally performed by a historically marginalized nomadic snake-charmer community, the dance embodies both aesthetic brilliance and socio-cultural struggle. This article examines Kalbeliya dance as an expressive form that negotiates marginality through rhythm and movement. By analyzing its rhythmic patterns, bodily vocabulary, and social context, the study highlights how Kalbeliya dance functions as a medium of cultural survival, resistance, and assertion of identity in contemporary India. The recognition of Kalbeliya dance by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage has further transformed its socio-cultural positioning, creating new opportunities as well as challenges for the community

title: Protest and pedagogy
abstract: Drawing from the rich cultural heritage and diverse historical contexts of Nepal, India, Sri Lanka, and Myanmar, we examine how teachers adapt traditional and modern pedagogical methods in response to linguistic and cultural diversity. Colonial legacies in Sri Lanka and Myanmar, along with Nepal’s shifting sociopolitical climate, offer insights into the evolving identities of educators amidst systemic educational changes. The role of civil protests is analyzed as a catalyst for educational transformation, with particular emphasis on recent teacher demonstrations in Sri Lanka, underscoring the potential of disruptive movements to spur positive change. This analysis aligns Fullan’s principles with South Asia's ongoing educational reforms, highlighting the resilience and adaptability of teachers in navigating cultural, historical, and political intersections.

title: Governance and Policy in Karnataka: A Comprehensive Analysis
abstract: This article provides an in-depth analysis of governance and policy-making in Karnataka, a state in southwestern India known for its cultural heritage and economic diversity. It examines the historical context of Karnataka’s governance, the administrative structure, and key policy areas such as education, healthcare, agriculture, infrastructure, and social welfare. The article highlights significant initiatives and programs implemented to enhance quality of life and promote sustainable development. Despite these advancements, Karnataka faces challenges including corruption, regional disparities, urbanization pressures, environmental sustainability, and ensuring inclusive growth. By exploring these aspects, the article underscores the importance of transparent, accountable, and participatory governance. It also emphasizes the need for continuous policy innovation and stakeholder engagement to address ongoing challenges and achieve equitable development in Karnataka.

title: A Study on the Factors Contributing to Tourism Attractiveness of Kashmir Valley
abstract: This study investigates the factors contributing to the tourism attractiveness of Jammu and Kashmir and their influence on tourist behavior and attitudes. title: DECLINING TRADITIONAL OCCUPATIONS IN KARNATAKA – A HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE
abstract: This paper examines the gradual decline of traditional occupations in Karnataka from a historical perspective. It explores how pre-colonial economic systems, colonial interventions, and post-independence modernization have contributed to the weakening of hereditary occupations such as weaving, pottery, leatherwork, folk performance, agriculture-based crafts, and nomadic services. The study highlights how industrialization, changing market demands, and urbanization have disrupted community-based livelihoods. It also analyzes the socio-economic consequences of occupational decline, including unemployment, migration, and loss of indigenous knowledge systems. The paper concludes that while modernization has created new opportunities, it has also endangered cultural heritage and traditional skills that once formed the backbone of Karnataka’s rural economy

title: Comparative Analysis of 3D Steel and Glulam Trusses Using ABAQUS
abstract: Abstract This study aims at developing an innovative and sustainable 3D truss system that can be applied in a variety of scenarios where intermediary propping is a hindrance. One prominent and pertinent application of such a system is in archaeological sites where long spans and no intermediary propping are desired. Previous research and studies have developed an innovative 3D steel truss for the same application. This study aims to further the innovation by providing a more sustainable alternative through Glulam and Glulam-Bamboo hybrid variations which are able to withstand similar loads as that of the steel truss but offering more sustainability and less impact on the environment as well as a light weight alternative. The results of such an alternative truss system are discussed here. One obvious problem faced with the alternative wood system was the large deflections observed and also certain regions with impermissible stresses. In addition, the proposed joint in the Glulam truss has been modelled and analyzed. It was found that the Glulam truss with lateral restraints at every quarter length of the span showed the best results in terms of deflection and stress developed. Also, the Glulam-Bamboo hybrid truss without any lateral restraints proved to be an equally effective alternative from a structural standpoint. The proposed joint system for the glulam truss also proved to be effective. The study concludes with a cost benefit analysis (CBA) between the steel, glulam and Glulam-Bamboo hybrid systems, which compares the viability of the proposed designs from an economic standpoint. The CBA shows that about 46% and 48% of costs are minimized on employing Glulam, Glulam- Bamboo respectively, instead of using Steel for the truss.

title: Tribal Contributions to Indian Culture: A Special Reference to Maharashtra
abstract: India’s cultural identity has been significantly shaped by its tribal communities, who constitute nearly 8.6% of the national population. Maharashtra, home to diverse tribes such as the Warli, Bhil, Gond, Katkari, Korku, and Thakar, presents a unique cultural mosaic that blends art, music, rituals, and ecological wisdom. Tribal contributions are visible in globally recognized art forms like Warli paintings, indigenous agricultural practices such as millet cultivation, vibrant folk dances, and nature-based festivals. This paper explores these contributions with special reference to Maharashtra, emphasizing their enduring impact on Indian cultural heritage. The study also highlights the challenges faced in preserving tribal traditions in the modern era, while underlining the need for documentation, policy support, and cultural promotion.

title: Asteroseismology in the Rubin/LSST Era
abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, named after astronomer Vera Rubin, promises to revolutionize our view of the dynamic night sky. Rubin’s 10-year survey, the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), will provide a unique optical time-domain view of the southern sky through repeated multi-band observations using the largest digital camera ever built. Although Rubin is not a dedicated asteroseismology mission, its combination of depth, sky coverage and long temporal baseline will enable large-scale studies of stellar variability across diverse Galactic environments, opening a new era of variability studies across the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. In this talk, I will briefly introduce Rubin-LSST and discuss its relevance for the asteroseismology community. Rubin’s strengths in probing faint and distant stellar populations will be highlighted, including applications to Galactic archaeology, stellar evolution, cluster studies and variability in the Magellanic Clouds and nearby dwarf galaxies. I will also discuss the challenges and opportunities of variability analyses using Rubin’s sparse and irregular cadence data. A major focus will be the complementarity between Rubin and current and future space missions. Synergies with TESS and PLATO will help extend variability studies to much larger stellar populations, while the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will provide important complementary capabilities in crowded and dust-obscured regions. I will briefly discuss Rubin’s role within the broader landscape of upcoming stellar astrophysics missions and surveys.

title: சகதம: சகதய (அனன பரசகத) மதனமக கடவளகக கணட வழபடம மற
abstract: Shakti worship is one of the most ancient and influential traditions within Indian religious systems. Archaeological evidence discovered in the Mohenjo-daro and Harappa civilizations (2600–1900 BCE) confirms the existence of mother goddess worship. Shaktism is defined as the religious path that accepts and worships Mother Parasakti as the Supreme Reality and the cosmic energy driving the universe. The Shakta religion believes that Shakti is the foundational energy behind the three cosmic functions: creation, preservation, and destruction. Concepts of Shakti are also found in Vedic texts, specifically in the Kausitaki Brahmana and the Taittiriya Samhita. The primary forms of Shakti worshipped include: • Durga (Protection) • Kali (Destruction) • Lakshmi (Wealth) • Saraswati (Arts/Knowledge) • Parvati (Love) All of these are regarded as different manifestations of the single, supreme Parasakti. While Shakti worship is prevalent across India in various forms, Amman worship in Tamil Nadu is deeply intertwined with the daily lives of the people. Rituals centered around Mariamman, Pongal, and the offering of Koozh (porridge) are unique highlights of Shakti worship in Tamil Nadu. Tantra and Mantra are integral components of Shakta worship. Considering Shakti to be the creative power of the Divine, this tradition views male deities as complementary counterparts to Shakti. It offers a unique, goddess-centric perspective as an alternative to traditional patriarchal religious structures. This article explores the origins, philosophy, diverse forms, worship methods, and ethical thoughts of Shaktism. In contemporary times, Shakta practices continue to hold immense significance through festivals like Navaratri and Dasara, as well as through vibrant Amman temples.

abstract: This paper examines the complex relationship between diaspora communities and heritage reconstruction processes, analyzing how displaced populations influence narrative construction and priority determination in heritage recovery initiatives. The analysis reveals that displaced communities operate as both preservers and innovators of cultural heritage, creating hybrid narratives that challenge traditional authenticity paradigms while establishing new frameworks for cultural continuity. title: Philosophical Anthropology of B. V. Markov. Part 1. Philosophy of the Era of “the Death of Man”
abstract: The article is devoted to the study of the Philosophical Anthropology of the recently deceased famous St. Petersburg philosopher Boris Vasilyevich Markov (1946-2023). Thanks to him, Russian Philosophical Anthropology started to develop actively in the 1990s. It is the peculiarities and significance of the philosophy of that period, are analyzed in the article. The writings of French philosophers, primarily the concept of the “death of man” by M. Foucault, were of central importance for the new Russian philosophy and Philosophical Anthropology of that time. The works of the archaeological and genealogical stages by Foucault had a great influence on Markov. The author of the current article examines in detail the significance of Foucault’s concept of the “death of man” and, in general, the understanding of man in Postmodernism for the development of Philosophical Anthropology of B. V.Markov in his works of the 1990s. To do this, the genesis and features of the development of European, primarily French, philosophy of the second half of the 20th century, presented in such concepts as episteme, deconstruction, archeology of knowledge, genealogy of power, language, are critically touched upon and analyzed. Based on these principles, Markov’s philosophical anthropology can be characterized as an archeology and genealogy of power in relation to man in culture, society and everyday life. The author emphasizes that the development of Philosophical Anthropology in the era of the “death of man” was a complex and controversial process, since such critical analytics led to the depersonalization of human being. The research presented in the article seeks to critically reveal the foundations of such an essentially anti-anthropological philosophy. Analysis of philosophy of B. V. Markov allows us to reveal its great significance for the development of domestic Philosophical Anthropology in the era of the “death of man”.

title: Maritime Silk Road Ceramics And Indian Ocean Networks, 200-1400 CE
abstract: This article reconstructs the maritime trade networks of the Indian Ocean between 200 BCE and 1400 CE through the ceramic evidence recovered from Southeast Asian port cities, shipwrecks, and burial sites. Drawing on archaeological assemblages spanning Indian Rouletted Ware, Tang-dynasty Changsha bowls from the Belitung shipwreck (c. 826 CE), Song-Yuan celadons and blue-and-white porcelains, and locally produced Thai and Vietnamese trade wares, the study traces the evolving structure of maritime exchange shaped by the monsoon wind system. The analysis challenges the conventional model of a unidirectional flow from advanced Chinese and Indian producers to passive Southeast Asian consumers. Instead, the ceramic record reveals that Southeast Asian entrepôts—Srivijayan ports, Philippine chieftaincies, and Javanese coastal polities—functioned as active agents in shaping demand, mediating redistribution, and assigning new cultural and political meanings to imported objects. The Belitung wreck demonstrates the industrial scale of ninth-century Chinese ceramic exports, while Philippine elite burial assemblages reveal the political instrumentalization of trade goods in competitive prestige economies. The article argues that no single maritime power dominated the Indian Ocean trade; rather, a shifting constellation of overlapping regional circuits, sustained by monsoon navigation, diverse shipbuilding traditions, and the complementary resources of ecologically distinct littoral societies, constituted an interconnected world economy in which Southeast Asian port cities were as essential as the kilns that supplied them.

title: Traumatic History and Transcultural Memory: A Reading of Numair Atif Choudhury’s Babu Bangladesh in the context of Nation formation
abstract: In the age of interdisciplinary studies Literary and Memory Studies is an emerging field of interest to young scholars and researchers. The manner in which Memory Studies interlink across various disciplines as history, geography, literature, psychology is worthy of exploring. Cultural memory entails convergence of fields such as cultural history, social psychology, media archaeology, political philosophy, comparative literature and relate past to the present. It is bifocal in nature since it leads to both remembering and forgetting. There are diverse ways in which Memory studies can be located in literary and media studies. My focus is to highlight how an exploration of memory studies further leads to a study of psychological trauma buried deep in the memory of an individual as well as its culture. The experience of undergoing the two World Wars, Holocaust, 9/11 episode, 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War, political strife in Afghanistan are major areas that can be studied with the aid of memory studies. I shall highlight on this specific area of memory studies by contextualizing how memory operates by its twin process of remembering and forgetting to bring out the trauma of the civilians of East Pakistan who had witnessed the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War. For this purpose Numair Atif Choudhary’s Babu Bangladesh (2019) is chosen to elucidate how the process of nation building is intrinsically connected to the present and past lives of its citizens. The narrative of formation of a new nation is continually questioned and reframed by the oral narratives of the generations of people who have witnessed its creation.

title: Symbolism and cultural identity: Documentation of cultural and religious motifs in Indian textiles
abstract: India’s textile heritage is one of the richest and most diverse in the world, deeply rooted in its textiles, crafts and art forms. Its diverse textile tradition can be seen in literary texts, temple sculptures, miniature paintings, and archaeological findings. Indian textiles inherit traditional and cultural motifs that reflect the country’s diverse culture, religious practices, beliefs, rituals and regional ideologies. Each region has cultivated its own distinctive textile identity, characterized by unique motifs that narrate local stories, myths, and cultural experiences. These motifs vary according to regional and geographical conditions. A motif, in the context of textile design, refers to a repeated decorative element or pattern that serves as a fundamental unit in art, design, or textiles. Religious motifs derived from faiths such as Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, Islam, and Sikhism play a vital role in Indian textile iconography. These motifs are not merely decorative but also carry symbolic meanings rooted in mythology, and nature. Symbols such as the lotus, conch, chakra, tree of life, peacock, and geometric Islamic arabesques illustrate the synthesis of faith and art in textile design, reflecting the spiritual and philosophical worldview of their creators. This paper explores the significance of traditional and cultural motifs in Indian textiles, tracing their historical evolution, regional variations, and symbolic meanings and their continuing relevance in contemporary design. By examining historical context, regional variations and modern interpretations this study highlights the enduring legacy and evolving trends of cultural and religious symbolism in Indian textiles.

title: The Vedic Era: Indian Women And Spirituality
abstract: this monograph, an attempt has been made to ascertain the spiritual state and spirituality of women in the Vedic period. The socio-religious status of women, their contribution and involvement in philosophical-intellectual debates, along with a comparison of Gender spiritual rights have also been revisited. Since the concept of spirituality has changed and grown over time, various definitions coexist today. Saints or enlightened ones have shown higher degrees of spiritual growth than the common man. The word "spirituality" has been used here to refer to a religious reforming process that comprises the examination of some universal concepts, such as compassion, love, generosity, afterlife, enlightenment, and truth. The Vedic civilization is an intriguing exception to the norm concerning the general situation of women becoming unsatisfactory as the years progressed. The role of women is increasingly gratifying the further back we look, including the spiritual realm. As a period of great social and political stability, the early Vedic era is regarded as the "golden age" of women. In contrast, the later Vedic era marked a sharp and apparent decline in the social standing of women. This work emphasizes the spiritual empowerment of women and highlights the crucial role they had in forming religious and cultural traditions during this time through a review of Vedic texts, academic interpretations, and archaeological data. The approach used in this work is strictly descriptive, and the data needed was gathered from primary as well as secondary sources with reference to Vedic women in antiquity. KEYWORDS- Vedic Era, Religion, Society, and Women’s Spirituality.

title: International Yoga Day 2026: Collective Harmony, Global Record
abstract: International Yoga Day, observed annually on 21st June, has evolved into a global celebration of health, harmony, and cultural heritage. In 2026, the event is distinguished by an ambitious attempt to set a Guinness World Record for the largest synchronized yoga performance. This editorial highlights the significance of the record as a symbol of collective consciousness, cultural pride, and global unity. Beyond the grandeur of numbers, the initiative underscores yoga’s role in preventive healthcare, inclusivity, and international recognition of India’s ancient wisdom. While the Guinness attempt adds historic value, the true essence of International Yoga Day lies in its continuity—encouraging individuals to integrate yoga into daily life for resilience, mindfulness, and holistic well-being. The editorial concludes that the record is not merely a milestone but a catalyst for sustaining yoga’s universal relevance in modern society.

title: Plant-wax biomarkers and their isotopes reveal complex relationships between climate, vegetation and fire during collapse of Indus Valley Civilization
abstract: Climate variability, especially monsoonal rainfall, has significantly shaped habitable areas for human populations in South Asia in the past just as it does today. Instances of climate-driven social disruptions and population movements are evident worldwide, as evidenced for example in the Classic Maya and the Indus Valley Civilization (IVC). However, climate change can manifest in very different ways in terms of vegetation and fire regimes, with important implications for regional environmental histories as well as socio-political patterns. As such, it is essential to develop a comprehensive understanding of the intricate interplay between climate, vegetation, fire, and archaeological evidence relating to changes in settlement patterns and continuities. Insights derived from such studies offer a foundation to explore and comprehend present and future human-environment interactions.Here we present multi-proxy time-series datasets derived from a 2.25-meter geological trench known as &#8216;Jankipura,&#8217; located within the semi-arid Thar Desert. Jankipura, located near Didwana Lake, holds prehistoric importance, being surrounded by major archaeological sites in the Thar Desert. It is also a part of the Didwana Palaeolithic Complex, surrounded by the IVC, Jodhpura-Ganeshwar, and Ahar-Banas cultural regions. The chronology of the Jankipura trench is constructed based on four 14C AMS dates ranging from 183 to 4656 cal yr. BP, aligning with the Mature phase of the IVC &#8211; a period characterized by population migration and a severe reduction in settlement density. Our analysis encompasses measurements of sediment total organic and bulk carbon isotope (d13Cbulk) composition, alongside examinations of plant-wax molecular distributions (n-alkanes and fatty acids). Additionally, we analyzed the &#948;13C and &#948;2H values of long-chain n-alkanes (C27, C29, C31, and C33) and fatty acids (C26, C28, C30, and C32) extracted from the sediment samples.Our study also involved the assessment of macro-charcoal concentrations (>125 &#181;m, differentiating grass from wood) to reconstruct the climate-vegetation-fire relationships during and after a major period of disruption of the IVC. The findings highlight an dry phase between 4656 and 2932 cal yr. BP, characterized by a mixed C3-C4 vegetational landscape with limited fire episodes. A significant fire episode took place during the period from 2932 to 1960 cal yr. BP, suggesting dry conditions supported by abundant C4 vegetation. Between 1960 and 183 cal yr. BP, three minor fire events occurred amid fluctuating rainfall conditions and a landscape dominated by mixed C3-C4 vegetation. The identified macro-charcoal predominantly comprised woody fragments over grass fragments. Notably, an increasing trend in isotope values, reaching its peak in macro-charcoal, is observed between 183 cal yr. BP and the present, signifying increased aridity compared to the mature phase of the IVC.Although the study is based on a single trench, our observation of a weak relationship between vegetation and fire suggests that the reconstructed fire events may have originated from anthropogenic activities. This sheds light on the significance of vegetation, especially the utilization of wood, during the Mature phase of the IVC. We recommend generating more records from this region to better comprehend the spatio-temporal interaction of the IVC population with the environment.

title: Decentralized Fund Management System for Indian Temples Powered by Blockchain
abstract: This research provides a proposal to integrate blockchain technology with a web application to come up with a solution for the fund management issues that the temples face. The main purpose of the research is to solve the problems of transparency, corruption and trust amidst donors and authorities of temple. Enabling the combination of a database management arrangement and a user-friendly website, a private blockchain was developed. The website is powered by smart contracts and serves as a solution that is capable of making fund operations accountable and visible. The outcomes of using this solution showed improvement in transparency, less corruption and increase of trust among donors. The temple authorities became more answerable and efficient as donors observed the movement of the donations in real time. This study gives a possible solution for temples to get the trust of their members back in order to ensure that the donations are properly implemented and a generation of cultural heritage is conserved.

title: Jagannath Temple, Puri
abstract: The venerable Jagannath temple, Puri is an embodiment of religious gastronomy tourism interwoven with sustainability. At the heart of the study is the sanctified Mahaprashada, whose entire life cycle was mindfully scrutinized to reveal its eco-conscious preparation, service and distribution, resulting in minimal environmental food print. Additionally, it elucidates the economic reverberations of Mahaprashada within the local community and its profound role in 'safeguarding the cultural heritage, fortifying communal identity and continuing the spiritual lineage'. Finally, in response to dynamic challenges like increasing tourism and modernisation, the research proposes avant-garde strategies to improve the sustainability of gastronomy tourism at the temple. Hence by positioning the Jagannath temple as a global exemplar of sustainable gastronomy tourism, the research can act as a blueprint for other religious sites trying to amalgam ancient gastronomic traditions with sustainability.

title: Exploring Local Colour in Pandit Lakhmi Chand’s Folk Literature
abstract: This research paper explores the concept of local colour which refers to the unique cultural practices, traditions, and customs of a particular region that distinguish it from other regions. The objective of this paper is to explore Indian philosophy and socio-cultural ethics through Haryanvi folklore, where an ideal society is imagined as an ordinary lifestyle. It highlights a ‘utopian’ vision through the importance of the local colour of Haryana and other regions to ensure that our cultural heritage is preserved for future generations. Moreover, its focus is on Pandit Lakhmi Chand’s use of local colour in a fictional presentation that reflects the customs, traditions, and beliefs and their preservation for generations for the people of Haryana. Through this examination, the paper offers insight into how local colour can enrich and enliven literature and how it can be used to reflect and celebrate the diversity of the human experience.

title: A Review on The Scientific Synthesis of the Saraswati River: Evidence from Remote Sensing, Geochemistry, and Ancient Texts
abstract: This work presents a multidisciplinary synthesis of scientific and textual evidence concerning the Saraswati River, a prominent feature in Vedic literature and a subject of long-standing historical and geological debate. The study integrates insights from remote sensing, sedimentology, isotopic geochemistry, and subsurface investigations to examine the existence, course, and characteristics of a paleo-fluvial system in northwestern India. Drawing upon satellite-based observations, particularly those conducted by the Indian Space Research Organisation, the study identifies extensive paleochannel networks consistent with a large, perennial river system extending from the Himalayan region toward the Rann of Kachchh. These findings are supported by lithological data obtained from drilling, which reveal sediment profiles indicative of high-energy fluvial processes typically associated with glacially fed river systems. The analysis further incorporates isotopic fingerprinting techniques to evaluate sediment provenance and distinguish between potential Himalayan and Siwalik sources. In addition, groundwater studies associated with these paleochannels are considered, highlighting their significance as long-term aquifer systems with substantial hydrological implications. By situating these scientific findings alongside references from Vedic texts, the work adopts an interdisciplinary framework to reassess the historical and geological status of the Saraswati River. The objective is not to assert definitive conclusions, but to consolidate existing lines of evidence and present a coherent synthesis that contributes to ongoing discussions in geoscience, archaeology, and environmental history. This contribution is intended as a research-oriented presentation aimed at fostering further scholarly inquiry and encouraging integrative approaches to the study of ancient river systems and their broader cultural and ecological contexts.

title: Ran-thok and Ling-chhom: indigenous grinding stones of Shertukpen tribes of Arunachal Pradesh, India
abstract: The Shertukpens are an Indigenous tribal group inhabiting the western and southern parts of Arunachal Pradesh, Northeast India. They are accomplished carvers of carving wood and stone. The paper aims to document the rich cultural heritage of grinding stone implements, Ran-thok (grinding stone) and Ling-chhom (nutting stone) used by the Shertukpens for grinding and nutting of cereal grains, fruits, rhizomes, and other food products. The study employed an interview-based survey followed by focused group discussion and observations during June and July 2019. A simple chaine operatoire was applied to understand the entire process of manufacturing grinding stones. The results reveal that the grinding implements are examples of endangered material culture, the use of which may produce better quality flour from both nutritional and gustatory perspectives.

title: Tradition and transformation: assessing the challenges and future of Sualkuchi handloom industry
abstract: Abstract The handloom industry of Sualkuchi is widely recognized for producing traditional Assamese textiles such as the mekhela chador and gamosa, which form a vital part of Assam’s cultural heritage and economic identity. Despite its historical and cultural importance, the sector is currently confronted with several challenges, including low remuneration for weavers, insufficient institutional support, scarcity of raw materials, limited innovation in product design, and intense competition from low-priced substitutes. Drawing on primary data collected from weavers and loom owners, the present study examines these challenges and evaluates the long-term sustainability of the industry. The findings indicate that without focused interventions—particularly in marketing, financial assistance, and diversification of products and designs—the Sualkuchi handloom industry may face serious difficulties in sustaining itself within an increasingly globalized economy.

title: Opportunities and Challenges of Indian Traditional Textiles in Viksit Bharat @2047
abstract: Indian traditional textiles represent a rich legacy of cultural heritage, indigenous knowledge, and sustainable artisanal practices. They contribute significantly to rural livelihoods, women’s employment, and India’s cultural economy. In the context of Viksit Bharat @2047, which envisions inclusive, sustainable, and self-reliant development, traditional textiles possess immense potential for economic growth, export promotion, and cultural diplomacy. However, the sector faces persistent challenges such as declining artisan participation, limited market access, technological stagnation, policy implementation gaps, and competition from mechanized and fast-fashion industries. This chapter critically examines the opportunities and challenges of Indian traditional textiles within the framework of Viksit Bharat @2047 and proposes strategic interventions to ensure the sustainable growth and global relevance of the sector by 2047.

title: The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute: A Study in the Context of Indian Knowledge System
abstract: The Indian Knowledge System (IKS) represents the accumulated intellectual traditions of India encompassing philosophy, literature, science, law, and spirituality preserved through ancient texts and manuscripts. The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) in Pune is one of the most important institutions dedicated to the preservation, study, and dissemination of this knowledge. Established in 1917 in honour of the eminent scholar Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar, the institute has become a global centre for Ideological research. Its vast manuscript collection and landmark projects such as the Critical Edition of the Mahabharata have significantly contributed to the study of Indian civilization. This research paper examines the role of BORI in promoting Indian Knowledge Systems through manuscript preservation, research activities, and academic publications. The study also highlights its contribution to cultural heritage and global scholarship.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Language, Culture, and Identity
abstract: The preservation of local languages is essential to maintaining cultural identity, yet many languages are rapidly declining due to globalization, technological advancements, and societal shifts. This study examines the role of university students in bridging the gap between language, culture, and identity through their involvement in language preservation initiatives. Focusing on students from fields such as linguistics, anthropology, history, and cultural studies, this research highlights their efforts to document, revitalize, and teach endangered languages. Through fieldwork, digital archives, and community outreach, these students contribute to the survival of languages that are integral to cultural heritage. The study also explores how language preservation fosters a deeper understanding of cultural values, traditions, and identity, offering a sustainable future for these languages. Ultimately, university students emerge as critical agents in the fight to preserve linguistic diversity for future generations.

title: The Goddess of Wisdom:May Irrigate Brains Again
abstract: A forbidden lifeline of ancient India on the banks of which the Vedas were composed by the sages while drinking the pure, fresh and fertile water of which river; that is the Goddess of wisdom, the Saraswati river. The legendary river once believed to be the cradle of ancient Indian civilization, vanished without a trace. For four centuries, its existence was rejected as a myth. However, modern archaeology and satellite imagery have uncovered its ancient route and reestablished its existence. This is the story of a lost river that shaped history and cannot be forgotten. Almighty and sacred river that was said to be the lifeline of ancient India. It was considered extinct and rejected as a legend. It was limited to hymns, songs, folk song and religious texts. But the earth remembers even that which history forgets. Saraswati was in its full glory till the composition of Vedas by Aryan’s on the banks of Saraswati in 6000 BCE (8000 years ago). Most of the sites of the Indus Valley civilization known so far are located on the Ghaggar - Hakra and its tributaries, not on the Indus river; hence it should be called ‘Saraswati Valley civilization’. This civilization was born 5,300 years ago on the banks of the Saraswati river and from there it spread to places like Harappa, Mohan Jo Daro etc. Both Saraswati and Vedic civilizations were flourished on the banks of river Saraswati. Saraswati dried up due to tectonic and climatic factors during the Mahabharata period. If its old route is revived then the desert can become heaven similarly the Goddess of wisdom may irrigate brains again.

title: Khatoozin – a naïve woman sculptor from Bagbasi village, Kurdistan
abstract: Khatoozin, a self-taught artist, embodies the essence of naïve art through her unique terracotta sculptures, which are deeply influenced by Kurdish mythology and her surroundings. Beginning her artistic journey at sixty, she drew inspiration from the rich cultural heritage of her region and the characteristics of local clay, allowing her imagination to flourish. Her sculptures, often depicting fantastical animal forms, reflect a spontaneous creativity marked by simplicity and a deep connection to nature. This paper explores the distinctive features of Khatoozin’s work, emphasizing the interplay of naïve artistic expression and cultural symbolism. By examining her representations of animals and the incorporation of local folklore, the study highlights the significance of her art in expressing a personal and communal identity, ultimately positioning her as a prominent figure within the naïve art movement.

title: Exploring The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on The Valuation of Antique Items In online Auction Platforms
abstract: This research explores the paradigm shift induced by artificial intelligence (AI) in the valuation of antique items within online auction platforms. Through the integration of sophisticated AI algorithms, the study meticulously examines the accuracy and efficiency of valuations, while also gauging user perceptions and their consequential impact on market dynamics. Comparative analyses with valuations conducted by human experts yield comprehensive insights into the reliability of AI-generated assessments. Ethical considerations, including transparency and bias mitigation, are thoroughly addressed. The findings underscore AI's transformative potential in revolutionizing antique valuation processes, shaping market trends, and enhancing user engagement. This study significantly contributes to our understanding of the dynamic interplay between AI technology and the preservation of cultural heritage in the evolving landscape of digital auctions

title: The Wesean Student Federation and the Unity of Northeast India: Examining the Role of Student Organizations in Fostering Cross-Border Solidarity in Wesea
abstract: This paper examines the formation and role of the Wesean Student Federation (WSF) within the broader context of the Northeast Indian region, often referred to as Wesea. The region, which includes parts of Northeast India, Bangladesh, and Myanmar, is characterised by its diverse indigenous populations, unique cultural heritage, and a history of political marginalisation. The study explores how the WSF has emerged as a unifying force for Wesean students, seeking to bridge ethnic divides and foster cross-border solidarity among the indigenous communities of Wesea. By analysing the WSF's e orts to address issues such as the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) and the abolition of the Free Movement Regime (FMR), this paper sheds light on the federation's role in advocating for indigenous rights, cultural preservation, and political sovereignty in a region marked by complex historical and geopolitical dynamics.

title: Ethics in archaeobotany: identifying current issues and initiating a declaration of principles
abstract: Abstract This article presents the first systematic assessment of ethical concerns specific to archaeobotanical research, focusing on principles and values. Conducted by an international group of archaeobotanists, the study used an anonymous online survey to document experiences and perceptions within the archaeobotanical community with the aim of raising awareness, identifying prevalent good practices and noting points for improvement. The questionnaire included ten thematic blocks and 63 main questions that covered regulations and guidelines, archaeobotany in excavations, funding, credit and authorship, intellectual property and right to access material, engagement with local communities, research obstacles, misconduct, ecological footprint, and dissemination of research results. We received responses from 114 participants, and the results highlight key challenges, including limited systematic recovery and study of plant remains, scarce funding, unclear decision-making authority, recurrent research misconduct, insufficient benefits for local communities, and low visibility of archaeobotanical research in dissemination and outreach. Building on these findings, we propose a declaration of principles tailored to archaeobotany, outlining the collective commitments of our community. This framework emphasizes safeguarding archaeological plant remains, ethical and rigorous research practices, and equitable participation. By adhering to these principles, archaeobotanists can promote scientific knowledge whilst fostering inclusivity, transparency, and respect for all individuals and communities involved or affected by our research. In this way, the initiative aims to strengthen archaeobotany as a discipline and cultivate a more ethical, inclusive, and collaborative research culture for both current and future generations of archaeobotanists.

title: Displaced trajectories: The evolution of boundaries in late prehistoric Europe
abstract: One of the most fundamental ways in which humans interact with their surroundings is by instantiating boundaries in the world, spanning from fully imagined boundaries to boundaries projected as concrete physical manifestations such as concrete fences and walls. The construction of physical boundaries requires basic cognitive abilities for spatial memory and mental imagery; as well as the practical ability to navigate existing environmental and social constraints in order to produce new ones. Therefore, a long-term cultural perspective on boundary construction, with a focus on the archaeological record, can reveal how artificial boundary structures emerge, and in turn how particular structured cultural environments scaffold cognition and social cooperation in a long-term perspective. This paper addresses the evolution of boundaries as a method of land division across north-western Europe in the 2nd -1st millennium BC. Based on more than 6000 dates of boundary features from a landscape and settlement context, it demonstrates how boundaries, at very different times in history, are introduced as ad-hoc, temporary enclosures of crops and livestock. Over centuries, the boundaries become increasingly materially and conceptually irreversible, and take on extensive forms of grid-like structures. These grids, spanning thousands of hectares, cause a permanent landscape fractioning. Furthermore, boundary structures begin to permeate other social domains, such as fences enclosing settlements or used as fortifications by larger social communities. These new boundaries obstruct movement along existing routes and they create visuospatial barriers, providing a new basic structure for humans to interact with and conceptualise their social and physical surroundings.

title: Maritime Silk Road Ceramics And Indian Ocean Networks, 200-1400 CE
abstract: This article reconstructs the maritime trade networks of the Indian Ocean between 200 BCE and 1400 CE through the ceramic evidence recovered from Southeast Asian port cities, shipwrecks, and burial sites. Drawing on archaeological assemblages spanning Indian Rouletted Ware, Tang-dynasty Changsha bowls from the Belitung shipwreck (c. 826 CE), Song-Yuan celadons and blue-and-white porcelains, and locally produced Thai and Vietnamese trade wares, the study traces the evolving structure of maritime exchange shaped by the monsoon wind system. The analysis challenges the conventional model of a unidirectional flow from advanced Chinese and Indian producers to passive Southeast Asian consumers. Instead, the ceramic record reveals that Southeast Asian entrepôts—Srivijayan ports, Philippine chieftaincies, and Javanese coastal polities—functioned as active agents in shaping demand, mediating redistribution, and assigning new cultural and political meanings to imported objects. The Belitung wreck demonstrates the industrial scale of ninth-century Chinese ceramic exports, while Philippine elite burial assemblages reveal the political instrumentalization of trade goods in competitive prestige economies. The article argues that no single maritime power dominated the Indian Ocean trade; rather, a shifting constellation of overlapping regional circuits, sustained by monsoon navigation, diverse shipbuilding traditions, and the complementary resources of ecologically distinct littoral societies, constituted an interconnected world economy in which Southeast Asian port cities were as essential as the kilns that supplied them.
