title: The Impact of Terrorism on Indian Tourism
abstract: Abstract This research article provides an in-depth, multi-dimensional examination of the complex relationship between terrorism and the tourism industry in India. Tourism serves as a foundational pillar of the Indian economy, contributing substantially to Gross Domestic Product (GDP), employment generation, and socio-economic development across diverse regions. However, the industry is inherently sensitive to perceptions of safety, stability, and geopolitical security. This paper investigates the immediate and long-term economic and psychological impacts of terrorist incidents on international tourist arrivals (ITA), domestic travel patterns, and revenue streams. By synthesizing historical data, analyzing pivotal case studies such as the 2008 Mumbai attacks, evaluating the nuances of modern "digital diplomacy," and examining the role of domestic tourism as a shock absorber, this study explores the systemic resilience of the Indian tourism sector. The findings suggest that while terrorism triggers significant short-term volatility and creates complex "spillover effects" on global risk perception, the Indian market exhibits high systemic resilience. This resilience is fundamentally driven by a robust domestic tourism base, proactive crisis management, and an evolving framework of "resilient branding." This paper ultimately argues that the future of Indian tourism depends on the sophisticated integration of advanced digital risk management, public-private partnerships (PPP), and a strategic move toward experiential and decentralized tourism models that decouple physical security incidents from destination perception. We further posit that true resilience requires shifting from a reactive posture—where policies are formed in the wake of trauma—to a proactive, integrated security-hospitality model that treats traveler safety as a core component of the "Incredible India" value proposition. This analysis aims to serve as a roadmap for stakeholders in managing the delicate balance between openness and security in an era of asymmetric threats. Keywords: Terrorism, Indian Tourism, Economic Impact, Security Perception, Crisis Management, Resilience, Tourism Policy, Destination Image, Soft Power, Digital Diplomacy, Risk Mitigation, Economic Multiplier, Experiential Tourism 1. Introduction The tourism industry is frequently categorized as a "peace-time industry," a designation that underscores the fundamental requirement of free, safe, and frictionless movement of people across borders. For a developing nation like India, which boasts immense cultural, historical, and geographical diversity—ranging from the high-altitude landscapes of the Himalayas to the tropical backwaters of Kerala—tourism is not merely an economic activity but a vital engine for national development and a primary instrument of soft power. It fosters infrastructure growth, provides direct and indirect employment to millions of individuals, and preserves diverse cultural heritages that might otherwise vanish in the face of rapid urbanization. Since the liberalization of the Indian economy in the early 1990s, the sector has grown exponentially, becoming a beacon for foreign investment and a cornerstone of the "Incredible India" brand, which has successfully marketed the country’s ancient heritage to a global audience. However, India has historically navigated a complex landscape of regional security and asymmetric threats, making it an ideal case study for examining the nexus between security and travel. This research seeks to provide a rigorous, evidence-based analysis of the causal link between terrorist activities and the tourism sector. It examines not only the immediate, observable fiscal losses but also the underlying dynamics that allow the sector to sustain itself—and eventually recover—amidst persistent, localized, and sometimes nationalized security threats. By exploring the triad of security, perception, and economics, this study aims to provide a strategic roadmap for policy makers, hospitality stakeholders, and international organizations to build a more secure, inclusive, and resilient future for Indian tourism. Beyond the immediate economic metrics, the scope of this study encompasses the social and psychological dimensions of travel security. As India seeks to position itself as a global leader in tourism, the ability to manage and mitigate the reputational damage associated with security incidents becomes a defining feature of a mature, globally competitive tourism market. This introduction sets the stage for a critical examination of how India has managed the transition from a passive, reactive posture to a sophisticated, technology-integrated, and proactive approach to tourism security. The evolution from a destination defined by its colonial history to one defined by modern dynamism necessitates a parallel evolution in how security and hospitality interact in the global public eye. The challenge is to maintain the allure of a vibrant, welcoming destination while simultaneously addressing the legitimate security concerns of international visitors, ensuring that the "Incredible India" narrative remains untarnished by the shadow of global instability. 2. Literature Review: The Theoretical Framework of Risk Academic literature on the tourism-terrorism nexus consistently highlights that the hospitality sector is among the most vulnerable to geopolitical instability. The relationship between terror and tourism is governed by several theoretical frameworks that explain how localized events translate into global industry shocks, creating a volatile environment where perception often outweighs physical reality. The Demand Side (Risk Perception Theory): Prospective international tourists, heavily influenced by global media cycles and government-issued travel advisories, often exhibit a heightened perception of risk. This leads to a rapid decline in demand for destinations associated with conflict, a phenomenon often described as the "cancellation effect." In the age of social media, this perception is amplified by the "geographic shadow" effect, where the perceived risk area extends far beyond the actual site of an incident, causing cancellations in regions that are geographically remote and objectively safe. Travelers often lack the granular geographical knowledge to distinguish between an affected urban center and a peaceful province thousands of kilometers away. This ignorance leads to a "blanket" risk assessment that disproportionately punishes unaffected regions. Cognitive biases, such as the "availability heuristic," further exacerbate this, where recent, vivid news reports override statistically objective safety data. The Supply Side (Operational Cost Inflation): Increased security requirements, higher insurance premiums for transport and hospitality, and the necessity of capital-intensive investments in surveillance technology drive up the operational costs for stakeholders. These costs squeeze profit margins, forcing providers to balance competitive pricing with elevated security standards. Often, the investment in "hard" security measures like metal detectors, perimeter walls, and X-ray scanners can create an institutionalized atmosphere of fear, which may indirectly detract from the guest experience by emphasizing the threat rather than the destination's appeal. This leads to the "securitization trap," where the effort to make a place safer makes it feel less like a leisure destination and more like a high-risk zone. The Crisis Management Lifecycle (CMLC): Modern scholarship suggests that destinations must navigate a cycle of mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery. In India, the challenge has historically been a reactive, rather than a proactive, approach. However, there is a clear shift toward "proactive resilience," where stakeholders are integrating crisis communication into their standard marketing strategies to maintain brand equity even during periods of volatility. This lifecycle approach emphasizes that recovery begins long before an incident occurs, through the building of strong stakeholder relationships, regular audits, and the establishment of transparent, real-time communication channels. It involves moving from a "crisis response" mindset to an "issue management" mindset. The Substitution Effect: Existing models suggest that international tourists rarely stop traveling entirely following a localized conflict; rather, they substitute their intended destination for one perceived as safer. The challenge for India, therefore, is to maintain its competitive position in the global tourism marketplace during periods of negative security narratives, ensuring that the "Incredible India" brand retains its allure as a preferred, rather than a risky, destination. By highlighting the unique experiences that cannot be replicated elsewhere, India seeks to raise the "cost of substitution," making the destination indispensable to the global traveler. The Social Amplification of Risk Framework (SARF): This framework explains how psychological, social, and institutional processes in the media can amplify or attenuate perceptions of risk. In the context of tourism, an incident is rarely just a physical event; it is a "communicated event." The way the media frames the event determines the longevity of the damage to the destination's image. SARF suggests that the "social station" of the victims and the "dread factor" of the attack method significantly influence the intensity of the public’s risk response, often leading to disproportionate and long-lasting avoidance behaviors. This framework is crucial for understanding why some regions struggle for years after a single incident, while others recover in months. title: The Role of Education in Shaping Social and Cultural Identity
abstract: Abstract Education serves as a foundational socialization agent, functioning simultaneously as a transmitter of cultural heritage and a critical catalyst for social evolution. This paper examines the intricate, recursive interplay between formal educational systems and the formation of both individual and collective identity. Through a comprehensive multidisciplinary analysis, it explores how curriculum design, teacher-student power dynamics, and the institutional culture of the school environment influence a learner’s perception of self, group belonging, and civic responsibility. The findings suggest that while education can foster national cohesion and cultural literacy, it frequently functions as a mechanism of exclusion for minority identities if pedagogical practices remain rigid or assimilationist. By synthesizing Social Identity Theory, Critical Pedagogy, and Bourdieu’s notions of cultural capital, this study highlights the urgent necessity for culturally responsive and pluralistic pedagogy in increasingly globalized societies. The article concludes by arguing that educational institutions must transition from engines of state-driven assimilation to platforms of pluralistic empowerment, where identity is treated as a fluid, dynamic, and multifaceted project. Keywords: Social Identity, Cultural Identity, Educational Policy, Socialization, Culturally Responsive Pedagogy, Critical Pedagogy, Inclusive Education, Bourdieu, Cultural Capital. 1. Introduction Education is rarely a neutral enterprise; it acts as both a mirror reflecting societal values and a laboratory for constructing future identities. As individuals navigate the formal pathways of schooling, they engage in a recursive process of internalizing cultural norms, linguistic registers, and social expectations. The institution of the school is, in effect, a microcosm of the state, exerting significant pressure on students to adopt specific worldviews while implicitly or sometimes explicitly others that fall outside the "ideal" citizen profile. The construction of identity within the classroom is not merely an incidental outcome of schooling; it is a foundational, if often obscured, objective of modern state-building. Historically, the advent of universal, compulsory schooling was designed to cultivate "ideal citizens"individuals who subscribe to a shared national narrative, often at the expense of regional, linguistic, or ethnic distinctiveness. This article investigates the systemic mechanisms both visible and invisible through which schools construct and constrain these identities. By examining the tension between nationalistic curricular agendas and the lived realities of increasingly diverse student populations, we can better understand how educational policy dictates the boundaries of belonging, exclusion, and democratic participation. As societies become more interconnected through digital technology and global migration, the role of education in navigating these complexities has never been more critical. We must look beyond simple academic attainment to understand how the school experience molds the architecture of the self, transforming the learner from a passive vessel into an agent of their own cultural synthesis. This study provides a deep dive into the psychological and sociological dimensions of this process, advocating for a pedagogical shift toward empowerment and plurality. 2. Theoretical Framework: The Anatomy of Identity in Education Social Identity Theory, pioneered by Henri Tajfel, posits that an individual’s sense of self is derived, in large part, from group membership. Educational environments categorize students, influencing their self-concept through two primary, interlocking vectors: The Formal Curriculum: This represents the "canon" of knowledge deemed valuable by the state. It dictates whose history is taught, whose literature is celebrated, and which scientific paradigms are validated. When this curriculum is narrow, students from non-dominant groups often perceive a painful disconnect between their home identity and the "official" identity promoted by the state, leading to a state of "double consciousness" described by W.E.B. Du Bois. This disconnect creates a cognitive barrier that can impede learning, as students must constantly mediate between the requirements of the school and the cultural authenticity of their home life. The Hidden Curriculum: Beyond the written textbooks, schools transmit values through unspoken norms, teacher expectations, and social behaviors. This "hidden curriculum" teaches students their place in the social hierarchy, reinforcing gender roles, class expectations, and ethnic prestige through the regulation of dress codes, disciplinary policies, and the physical architecture of classrooms. The subtle messages conveyed by who is praised, who is disciplined, and what is considered "proper" behavior collectively shape the student's internal map of their own social viability. Furthermore, we must integrate Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of "cultural capital." Educational systems tend to reward the cultural capital of the dominant classsuch as mastery of standard linguistic registers and familiarity with bourgeois cultural referencesplacing those from marginalized backgrounds at a distinct structural disadvantage. This necessitates an inquiry into how schools can transition from reinforcing existing inequities to dismantling them through critical pedagogy. As Paulo Freire argued, education must move away from the "banking model" of rote memorization, where students are passive vessels, toward a problem-posing methodology that validates the student’s lived experience as legitimate knowledge. By situating the classroom as a field of struggle, educators can help students decode the systemic forces that shape their identities, thereby fostering agency rather than resignation. The goal is to move toward a model of "transformative education" that views student identity as a site of potentiality rather than a deficit to be corrected. 3. The Psychology of Linguistic Displacement In many post-colonial and multicultural nations, the medium of instruction often conflicts with the learner’s home language, leading to profound identity friction. Research indicates that when schools privilege colonial or dominant languages at the expense of indigenous or heritage tongues, students frequently experience "linguistic alienation." 3.1 The Process of Alienation When a student’s primary tool for communicationtheir mother tongueis excluded from the academic environment, they are effectively told that their home culture lacks academic legitimacy. This leads to a fragmented cultural identity where the student feels compelled to perform a "school persona" that is divorced from their domestic life, often resulting in lower academic self-esteem and cultural estrangement. The school, in this scenario, functions as a site of symbolic violence, where the student's background is not merely ignored but actively invalidated. This alienation is compounded by the psychological toll of being forced to choose between linguistic assimilation and academic success, a choice that fundamentally fractures the self-concept. 3.2 Case Study: The Kura Kaupapa Māori Experience The success of bilingual integration is exemplified by initiatives such as the Kura Kaupapa Māori in New Zealand. By teaching through the medium of the indigenous language and embedding traditional Māori cultural practices into the daily curriculum, these schools demonstrate significant benefits in student outcomes. Research confirms that preserving heritage language is essential not just for cultural survival, but for stable psychological development. These programs illustrate that allowing the "home voice" to coexist with the "school voice" creates a bridge, enabling students to traverse multiple cultural worlds with confidence rather than conflict. By centering Te Aho Matua (the foundational philosophy of these schools), educators have successfully demonstrated that cultural grounding is a prerequisite for, not an obstacle to, academic achievement. This model provides a blueprint for global efforts to reclaim linguistic sovereignty within the classroom. 4. Discussion: Navigating the Globalized Challenge The contemporary challenge for educators is to balance the need for a shared national identityoften required for civic cohesion with the necessity of preserving diverse cultural backgrounds. Globalization has introduced new dimensions to this debate; students now navigate hybrid identities in a digital landscape that is both local and transnational. Additive Bilingualism: Policies that encourage proficiency in both the national/global language and the mother tongue yield the most stable identity outcomes. This prevents the "subtractive" effect where academic gain comes at the cost of cultural loss. Representational Narratives: Historical curricula must move beyond "single stories." When students see their communities reflected accurately in history and literature, their civic participation increases. This requires not just tokenistic inclusions but a systemic shift in how we narrate the nation’s history to include subaltern voices. title: Editorial: Enhancing the social skills and social competence for children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder
abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is characterized by early-onset differences in social communication and interaction that frequently continue across the lifespan [1], [11]. These challenges may influence social reciprocity, pragmatic language, adaptive functioning, and overall well-being [1]. When not addressed through appropriate intervention, social difficulties can intensify over time, potentially limiting community participation and interpersonal development [11].Recent epidemiological reports indicate that ASD prevalence continues to rise. According to 2023 data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), approximately 1 in 36 eight-year-old children in the United States has been identified with autism, reflecting a substantial increase compared to earlier estimates [2], [10]. Comparable data from China suggest a prevalence rate of roughly 0.7% among children aged 6 to 12 years [2], [10].This Research Topic seeks to advance understanding of how social development unfolds in individuals with ASD and to examine intervention models tailored to individual profiles [11].The included studies investigate cognitive, neural, and behavioral dimensions of autism, while also addressing contextual factors such as family engagement, sensory processing differences, and co-occurring emotional conditions including anxiety and depression [1], [11]. By connecting empirical findings with applied practice, the collection contributes to a broader conceptual framework for strengthening social competence in autistic youth.A prominent focus of this Research Topic involves structured programs designed to foster social functioning. These approaches range from structured psychosocial programs to emerging biomedical techniques, reflecting the growing diversity of intervention strategies in the field.Mairena et al. [1] conducted a randomized, waitlist-controlled pilot trial evaluating an adapted Social Adjustment Enhancement Intervention Program (SAEIP). Implemented within a university-affiliated public mental health hospital, the project aimed to demonstrate the feasibility of delivering structured, evidence-informed services within publicly funded systems.Seventy-nine autistic participants between 8 and 17 years old completed the 10-session group intervention. Social behavior changes were measured using structured observational methods, while parent-report questionnaires assessed internalizing symptoms [1].The results indicated meaningful gains in eye contact and functional communication among younger participants and those with higher verbal intelligence. In addition, reductions in internalizing symptoms were observed within the intervention group. Although statistical significance was not achieved across the entire sample, the direction of change consistently favored the intervention. These findings underscore the importance of tailoring interventions to individual developmental and cognitive profiles while also demonstrating the feasibility of implementing such programs in public service settings. [1].Barron et al. [5] examined the broader impact of therapeutic horsemanship (TH), an animal-assisted intervention, with particular attention to caregiver outcomes. While benefits for autistic children have been documented, research exploring secondary effects on caregivers remains limited.In this 16-week pilot study, 13 caregiver-child dyads participated in structured TH sessions [5]. A mixed-methods design combined quantitative assessment with qualitative interviews. Results demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in caregiver stress (p = 0.03) as measured by the DASS-21 scale. Interview data further revealed recurring themes related to service navigation challenges, financial strain, and limited support resources. Importantly, caregivers described reduced emotional burden as their children engaged in TH, suggesting that intervention benefits may extend to the entire family system and highlighting the importance of incorporating caregiver outcomes in intervention research [5].Cheng et al. [4] presented a case study exploring low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation (tFUS) as a novel therapeutic avenue. Currently, no pharmacological treatment directly targets the core social and behavioral characteristics of ASD.In this report, tFUS was administered to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of a child with ASD for 30 minutes daily across four weeks (20 sessions total) [4]. Clinical rating scales and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) were used to monitor outcomes. Improvements were observed in social interaction and repetitive behaviors, alongside increased functional connectivity involving the primary somatosensory cortex. While these results are preliminary and based on a single case, they suggest that modulation of cortical activity may offer a promising complementary strategy for addressing core ASD features [4].Understanding ASD requires attention to both biological substrates and contextual influences, which together shape behavioral expression.Sun et al. [10] applied a machine learning-based multi-stage feature refinement approach to identify structural brain characteristics distinguishing individuals with ASD from typically developing peers. The study included 175 autistic participants and 69 controls aged 7-18 years.Nine structural features were identified as particularly discriminative, many associated with neural circuits involved in reward processing, including hippocampal subregions [10].Alterations within these systems may contribute to differences in social motivation and engagement, offering insight into the neurobiological underpinnings of ASD.In addition to structural brain differences, environmental factors such as sleep patterns also play a critical role in shaping social and behavioral outcomes.Chen et al. [7] investigated the association between social jet lag (SJL)-a misalignment between biological rhythms and social schedules-and core autism symptoms in young children.Nearly half of the sampled children (49.8%) experienced sleep difficulties, with marked differences between weekday and weekend sleep patterns [7]. Among children aged 2-3 years, greater SJL was positively correlated with more pronounced core symptoms. These findings underscore the potential impact of circadian regulation on behavioral expression and highlight the importance of consistent sleep routines.Social functioning is closely linked to language use, especially narrative and pragmatic skills.Landau et al. [3] explored storytelling ability in autistic individuals and their first-degree relatives to examine possible associations with the Broad Autism Phenotype. Participants completed both visually supported storytelling ("First Telling") and unsupported retell tasks.Across groups, retell narratives were generally less elaborated. Notably, patterns of narrative performance overlapped between autistic participants and their relatives, suggesting subtle familial influences. The removal of visual cues appeared to amplify pragmatic challenges, mirroring conversational demands in everyday contexts [3].Building on these findings, recent work has also explored how such communicative abilities can be reliably assessed using remote technologies.Communication (e-ABaCo). Thirty autistic adolescents (15 assessed remotely, 15 in person) were compared to typically developing controls.Results demonstrated strong equivalence between remote and face-to-face administration.Both autistic groups showed distinct pragmatic profiles relative to controls. The study supports telehealth as a valid and accessible modality for pragmatic assessment [8].Research on autism is increasingly expanding beyond clinical and behavioral domains to include environmental design and large-scale knowledge synthesis. Together, these approaches contribute to a broader understanding of how social participation can be supported across different contexts.Qian et al. [2] employed structured user-centered design models to create museum environments responsive to the needs of autistic children. Using the Kano model, Quality Function Deployment, and the PUGH matrix, the researchers identified design priorities.An interactive science and technology museum model incorporating AR/VR elements and spatial guidance yielded the highest satisfaction ratings, with approximately a 23% improvement in user satisfaction [2]. The study illustrates how systematic design processes can enhance engagement and accessibility.Complementing these applied design approaches, Qiao et al. [9] provided a broader perspective through bibliometric analysis of autistic traits research spanning 1997-2024. The review of 1,044 publications revealed steady growth in scholarly output, with significant contributions from England, the United States, and Australia.The field has expanded beyond genetic and behavioral paradigms to incorporate environmental, hormonal, and psychiatric dimensions, reflecting increased recognition of autism's heterogeneity [9]. This shift reflects a growing recognition of autism as a complex and heterogeneous condition, reinforcing the need for interdisciplinary research and practice.Fan and Ko [6] provided qualitative insight into the lived experiences of Chinese caregivers of children with ASD. Four recurring themes emerged: the enduring hope for typical development, tension between expectations and reality, progression through emotional adjustment phases, and resilience in daily caregiving.These findings highlight the cultural shaping of parental experiences and emphasize the need for context-sensitive support services. They also underscore the importance of integrating caregiver perspectives into intervention planning, policy development, and service delivery.The collective findings point toward several important directions for future research. These priorities reflect the need for more integrative, longitudinal, and context-sensitive approaches to understanding and supporting social development in autism:• Longitudinal evaluation of psychosocial and biomedical interventions [1], [4] • Greater emphasis on individualized, profile-based intervention planning [1], [11] • Further investigation of reward system alterations and social motivation [10] • Expanded family-centered outcome research [5], [6] • Cross-cultural comparative studies [6], [11] These priorities highlight the importance of advancing interdisciplinary research that bridges clinical practice, neurobiological mechanisms, and real-world contexts of care.This Research Topic illustrates the inherently multidisciplinary nature of autism research. The studies span clinical trials, neurobiological investigations, remote assessment innovations, environmental design strategies, and caregiver narratives. Together, they reinforce the understanding that enhancing social competence in ASD requires coordinated attention to biological mechanisms, environmental structures, and family well-being. By refining evidencebased practices and promoting inclusive systems, this body of work contributes meaningfully to advancing participation and quality of life for individuals on the autism spectrum.The following

title: A STUDY OF RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN TRADE RELATED ASPECTS OF INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS AND BIO-DIVERSITY: EMERGING ISSUES
abstract: A STUDY OF RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN TRADE RELATED ASPECTS OF INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS AND BIO-DIVERSITY: EMERGING ISSUES Introduction: The topic of intellectual property rights has gained more and more attention from the general public in recent years. Economically and politically, intellectual property rights (IPRs) have never been more important or controversial than they are now. This is because, under the auspices of the World Trade Organization’s Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights, most developing countries have swiftly adopted more stringent protections for intellectual property (TRIPS Agreement). This topic comes up frequently in discussions and debates on a wide range of subjects, including but not limited to genetic resources, biotechnology, traditional knowledge, biopiracy, farmers’ rights, food security, and public health. Given the wide-ranging societal and economic effects of IPRs, it is important to view their protection in terms of economic growth and in the broader context of sustainable development. One of the most contentious issues in the debate over biodiversity management at the national and international levels is the allocation of property rights due to the growing economic importance of biological resources and the question of ownership of these resources. This is directly associated with the rise of genetic engineering and the tremendous business prospects it offers. In many cases, citizens of one country are given the right to protect their intellectual property (IP) over resources of another country that were derived from genetic research. In this area, there is a significant discrepancy between the ownership structures of developed and developing nations. While developing nations protect their own claims to the majority of the world’s remaining biodiversity and natural resources, developed nations house the vast majority of the world’s genetic engineering research capacity. They are enthusiastic supporters of expanding monopolistic intellectual property rights to encourage the commercial exploitation of biodiversity and related inventions. These transformations have prompted states to re-evaluate their intellectual property rights regimes in light of new conflicts over who owns biodiversity and the associated body of knowledge. For all intents and purposes, the Convention on Biodiversity (CBD) is the primary treaty addressing biodiversity conservation and management. Plant genetic resources are a “common heritage” of humankind. The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (PGRFA Treaty) calls on all countries to share their genetic resources with the rest of the world. When it comes to establishing a legal framework for the protection of plant varieties, the International Convention for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV Convention) is crucial. A number of other international instruments also address the management of biodiversity. Biological resources are only peripherally related to the TRIPS Agreement. There is an ongoing discussion about how the Convention on Biological Diversity’s goals relates to intellectual property rights. The impact of the TRIPS Agreement on achieving the CBD’s goals and sustainable development, in general, is a contentious topic. Trademarks, patents, copyrights, industrial designs, and geographical indications are the primary legal tools for safeguarding intellectual property rights. In addition to the aforementioned forms of protection, sui generis (meaning “of its own”) forms of protection have developed to meet the unique requirements of knowledge creators. Since farming has always been predicated on the principle of knowledge sharing, IPRs have never been particularly relevant to the agricultural sector. Genetically modified plant varieties are just one example of the remarkable agricultural innovations that have occurred in the last few decades. Agriculture and food security are inextricably linked, making the implementation of IPRs in agriculture particularly important. Can intellectual property rights help ensure people have access to nutritious food? Can they be considered justifiable? Developing countries continue to worry a great deal about their ability to provide adequate food for their populations. Recent advances in our understanding of biodiversity’s benefits have highlighted the value of traditional knowledge (TK). Proponents of the current systems of intellectual property rights argue that, when combined with benefit-sharing arrangements, IPRs provide incentives for continued investment by local and indigenous communities in the preservation of their biodiversity-related cultural heritage. The potential for theft of indigenous knowledge is exacerbated by current intellectual property rights (IPR) systems like patents. Concerns about the misuse of IPR laws have been exacerbated by acts of biopiracy, such as the US patenting of the medicinal properties of turmeric and Neem, which have been used for centuries in India. An increasing amount of attention is being paid at the global level to the relationship between medical patents and the human right to health. Questions about whether or not drugs can and should be patented have become central to discussions about drug access. One of the most significant changes in the law for developing countries that are WTO members is the expansion of patentability in the health sector, which is codified in the TRIPS and has prompted a significant outcry in a number of developing countries where access to medicines is already abysmally low. One specific issue that needs addressing is the connection between IP protection and environmental management. The rise of biotechnology and the risk of creating GMOs have both undermined efforts to preserve the natural world. One of the long-standing tenets of sustainable development is the necessity of EST transfer to developing countries. Protecting intellectual property is essential to achieving long-term sustainability, as is ensuring equitable access to its fruits. The developed world has advocated for intellectual property rights (IPRs) in international policy forums, while the developing world has voiced concern about the impact of IPRs on technology transfer. A country like India’s biodiversity, traditional knowledge protection, food security, right to health, and sustainable development are all directly affected by the assertion of intellectual property rights and the resulting private monopolies over biological resources. The international intellectual property rights (IPR) regime, of which many aspects are still evolving, directly impacts India’s IPR regime. India’s domestic legislation and ground practices will be influenced by how the country handles these rapid international developments. As a signatory to numerous international treaties and pacts, India must adopt or revise appropriate national legislation to meet the challenges posed by globalisation. Laws pertaining to intellectual property rights and biodiversity include the Biological Diversity Act of 2002, as amended in 1999, 2002, and 2005; the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights (PPVFRAct) Act of 2001, as amended in 1999, 2002, and 2005; the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act of 1999, and the Seeds bill of 2004 to replace the Seed Act of 1966. An area of intense interest and difficulty in the ‘international fora’ is the function and effect of IPRs in managing biodiversity and sustainable development. Thus, to comprehend its growing importance and role in formulating national strategies for sustainable development, it is necessary to understand and appreciate the social, cultural, and techno-economic foundations of intellectual property systems, the nature of these systems, and the rationale for protecting them. Objectives of the Study: The primary goal of the research is to give a thorough background material on the connection between the TRIPS Agreement’s provisions and biodiversity and to discover strategies to compromise the competing concerns. Here are some of the other objectives of the study: 1. To examine the connection between intellectual property rights (IPRs) and the TRIPS system’s goals of promoting the protection, sustainable use, and fair distribution of the world’s biological diversity and the advantages of doing so. 2. Some difficulties in expanding IP protection to include Agro-biodiversity are also discussed, including life-sciences patents and plant-variety protection. 3. Analyse the TRIPS rules as they protect traditional knowledge and focus on food security as a whole. 4. Analysis of the influence of the international legal framework under TRIPS on India’s legal system; the applicable legislation in India; and how to strike a balance between CBD and TRIPS to encourage financial growth while sustaining biological and social variety for the sake of food & health-security. 5. To provide strategies for addressing these difficulties and the next steps for addressing each issue at the national and global levels. Scope of The Study The scope of research is wide, such as TRIPS-Agricultural Issues; TRIPS-Biotechnology Issues; TRIPS-Public Health; TRIPS-Traditional Knowledge, plants and life forms; Geographical Indication Issues; but this research work includes the issues and relationship between the TRIPS and Agriculture, food security and Traditional knowledge and human health. title: Research Briefs through Interpreters’ Eyes: Recommendations for Scientists Sharing Park‐Based Research
abstract: Today’s scientists and science communicators have to navigate a complex and rapidly changing media environment (National Academies 2016). Americans are divided along party lines in terms of how they view the value and objectivity of scientists. In particular, there are sizable gaps between Democrats and Republicans when it comes to trust in scientists whose work is related to the environment (Funk et al. 2019). In a media landscape pocked with skepticism and false claims, partnerships with trusted institutions are valuable and critical (Nesbit 2014, Skorton 2018). Intermediaries like docents, interpretive rangers, and guides who work in museums, zoos, and aquariums win high marks for trust among public audiences. These interpreters have the potential to increase the public’s perception of the value of scientific research (National Research Council 2009, Schneider 2017). As truth is replaced with true-sounding “post-facts,” it is critical for science to advance the most accurate knowledge (Plavén-Sigray et al. 2017). One way to do so is to maximize its accessibility to non-specialists. However, scientists and interpreters face time constraints that limit opportunities for in-depth, face-to-face exchanges about place-based studies. Furthermore, scientists’ published, peer-reviewed articles are often not accessible to professional audiences outside academe (Merson et al. 2017). With readability of scientific texts decreasing (Plavén-Sigray et al. 2017), research briefs are a valuable and reasonable compromise. Briefs are produced across disciplines. Here, we focus on their features and usability within the National Park Service (NPS). As explained on NPS websites, 18 research learning centers and 32 regional offices of the Inventory & Monitoring (I&M) Division support science scholarship and communicate park-relevant findings. Lengthy technical reports do not meet the needs of all audiences; hence, they produce resource briefs: “concise highlights of monitoring findings in a visually appealing format that are directed towards a wider range of NPS staff” (Mims et al. 2016). Briefs are vetted by scientists and staff with disciplinary expertise, making them reliable sources of information which convey essential facts to their readers. The OASLC staff collaborates with park staff from a variety of disciplines as well as natural resource staff with Alaska's Southeast and Southwest Inventory and Monitoring Networks (I&M) in developing and providing resource briefs. … The OASLC works with park and I&M staff in determining who the main audience will be when drafting these resource briefs, as well as working with staff in order to determine the best ways to disseminate resource brief information (for example: websites, interpretive training, and/or presentations). The OASLC posts current and past resource briefs on the OASLC website, as well as links to where these briefs are housed on park and I&M sites (available online; referred to on March 25, 2020).1 In this article, we focus on the format preferences and priorities of an essential group of potential users of research briefs. We contend that slight changes in the typical format and content will make briefs more useful to docents, volunteers, and interpretive rangers (hereafter all referred to as interpreters) who are in a position to communicate science in parks, nature centers, and other informal learning environments. The parks where they work function as our nation’s valuable outdoor laboratories, an underappreciated aspect of protected land (Shea 2015, Char et al. 2020). Discussing place-based, ecological studies is a natural fit for park interpreters. The National Association for Interpretation defines interpretation as “a mission-based communication process that forges emotional and intellectual connections between the interests of the audience and the meanings inherent in the resource.” The tag line is even more explicit about the place-based nature of interpretation: If you help visitors learn about a place that’s important to you, you’re an interpreter (National Association for Interpretation 2020). In the name of advancing the public’s understanding of park-based science, Interpreters and Scientists Working on Our Parks (iSWOOP, NSF DRL-1514776) project leaders have worked to promote partnerships between scientists and National Park Service interpretive rangers. iSWOOP did so mainly by coordinating on-site and online professional development opportunities. However, we were also curious to gauge interpreters’ impressions of briefs as another avenue for increasing the accessibility of relevant research. To do so, we needed to understand both what interpreters encounter when they consult briefs and how they use them. We downloaded and analyzed features of existing briefs from Park Service websites and conducted interviews with a convenience sample of interpreters. Because our goal was to arrive at a format that would be most supportive of interpreters’ efforts to highlight the value and relevance of park-based research, the semi-structured interviews included a hypothetical situation and task as well as questions about interpretive practice. To gauge their impressions of briefs, we offered two versions of a brief, one traditionally formatted brief and one with a shorter title, sub-headings with questions to pique curiosity, and a first page with half the space allocated to photos (Fig. 1, complete versions of the briefs are included in Appendix S1). One researcher conducted in-person, semi-structured interviews with individuals and pairs of NPS interpreters. An effort was made to pair resource management staff who might have different strategies and lenses for the briefs with interpreters with 3–5 years of experience. In this group of interpreters, one would expect mastery of the basics of the job, capacity to take on a challenge, and several hours each workday spent interacting with the public. Ultimately, interviewees included interns and research learning center staff as well as interpreters focusing on social media rather than in-person interpretation. Interviewees had a range of experience and backgrounds (years with NPS ranged from nine months to 30 years and a mix of degrees including science education, ecology, archeology, criminal justice, graphic design, and biology). In this article, we focus on the reactions of five experienced interpreters whose job responsibilities included formal and informal interpretive interactions with the public. The five included two male and three female frontline interpreters with 3–8 years interpreting for the National Park Service. In order to understand interpreters' impressions of the format and content of research briefs, we prepared two versions of a brief summarizing a study of the impact of climate change on amphibians in northwest Indiana (Appendix S1). The briefs drew on annual reports submitted by a herpetologist researching amphibian abundance in the Midwest. The timing of breeding at field sites across northwest Indiana illustrated the value of parks as an outdoor laboratory. An NPS science coordinator had authored and shared her draft (but retired before finalizing and publishing it). iSWOOP staff updated the format to resemble published briefs. Version 1 was the more traditional. Its sub-headings included: Importance, Methods, Preliminary Results, Future Research Directions, and Implications for Park Management. iSWOOP staff used the content from Version 1 to create Version 2, giving it a shorter title (Frogs and Salamanders of Indiana Dunes), sub-heads in the form of questions (such as Methods: How did scientists determine an answer?), and large photos with a researcher and salamander on page 1 in place of the map and graph that appeared on Version 1 (Fig. 1). Audio- and video-recorded interviews ranged from 35 to 75 minutes. About half the total interview time was dedicated to a think-aloud protocol. The interview began with a question about the interpreter’s background and a question about what they found most rewarding in interpreting science. Rangers were then asked to imagine they were new at a park that wanted to increase interpretation of park-based research on amphibians (Appendix S2). The wording of the task (Fig. 2) was meant to elicit interpreters’ professional and practical needs as they imagined interpreting the information for the public. Interviewees could choose one of two briefs on offer. While looking over Versions 1 and 2, interpreters were asked why the one they selected appealed to them and to comment as they read. Interpreters verbalized their thoughts as they perused, read, or skimmed the brief of their choice (Nielsen 2012). After completing the read-through, interpreters answered open-ended questions about how they could use the information they had gleaned in an interpretive interaction: What they would use as a hook for capturing the attention of visitors and how they would establish relevance for audience members of different ages. These open-ended, semi-structured interview questions related to interpretive practice: knowledge of audience for capturing interest and making the content relevant; knowledge of the resource for confidence with the content; and the personal rewards of interpretation. Finally, interpreters were asked to use a 10-point scale rating: How confident would you feel talking about this topic with visitors for less than 5 minutes, 5–10, or more than 10 minutes? We created transcripts based on notes and audio recordings. Utterances from the think-aloud portion of the interview were grouped into three categories: Format/Layout, Text, and Images. Utterances were then coded according to their positive or negative valence. Responses such as “nice” and “useful” were coded as positive. Critiques, expressed lack of clarity, and indications of disengagement (“This picture is dark,” or “I can’t make out the axes,” or “I didn’t feel like reading more”) were coded as negative. Descriptive codes were developed based on responses to open-ended, semi-structured interview questions related to interpretive practice (Charmaz 2006; Hsiung 2010). We also used a set of a priori categories related to interpretive craft, for example, emotional and intellectual connections, hooks, and relevance. Emerging themes were signaled by repeated use of phrases (Saldaña 2015). When interpreters do seek out research briefs, what do they encounter? To understand the common features and variation among existing briefs, we created a sample from the pool of briefs made available by the NPS I&M networks’ regional websites. From the 32 regional I&M home pages, we navigated to Reports and Publications. The dropdown menus then vary. We selected Briefs and Summaries. If that was not an option, we chose Quick Reads. If neither option appeared, the region is not represented. We selected briefs on wildlife and plant species because of public interest in seeing wildlife and iconic plant species. Two researchers developed and tested the protocol for reviewing existing briefs, making determinations such as whether to count text in captions or not (which we did). We established categories based on features like readability that affect access, the presence of visuals and stories because use of visuals and stories are popular interpretive techniques, and relevance, which is seen as tied to interpreters’ mission to form intellectual and emotional connections (Ham 1992). The interviews and first round of our analysis of briefs occurred concurrently. Because interpreters spoke to the complexity of graphs and usefulness of photos, we refined our assessment by coding for different types of graphs and the percentage of space allocated for visuals. In addition, we created codes for the purpose of images, for example, sets the scene, shows the researcher in action, displays a resource or phenomenon that is rarely seen. We looked at a number of characteristics of briefs, including use of images and figures, story elements, relevance, and readability, as these elements commonly inform interpretive interactions. The 61 briefs collected were reviewed for readability. On the Flesch reading ease scale, the higher the score (0–100), the more readable the text. The scale takes into account the average number of words in a sentence and the average number of syllables per word (McGovern 2019). We found a range of a range from 10 to 66 with a mean score of 34.5. Fifty-three of the briefs scored “very difficult” (0–30, which may be comparable to reading The Affordable Care Act), or “difficult,” (30–50, which may be comparable to reading an academic paper on chess) (McGovern 2019). Just one scored in the range considered plain English (60–70, an eighth or ninth grade reading level), while five could be considered appropriate for high school students (50–60). Half of the briefs explicitly addressed the “importance” of the topic or research efforts. Though we planned to count briefs with a story arc and expected to code for one of three archetypal conflicts (good vs. evil, unanticipated connections, and breakthroughs), just one brief had an identifiable narrative. Images are a large part of most research briefs. By images we mean graphic elements including figures, maps, and photos. We estimated space given to graphic elements (by the quarter page). Of 61 briefs collected from inventory and monitoring projects, authors typically gave graphic elements more than 25% and less than 50% of the space. All of the briefs featured at least one image. These typically served roles including providing visual interest, illustrating text, or describing trends with photos, maps, and graphs. Although nine briefs included 6–10 visual elements, the mode was just two (16 briefs of 61). We coded for images that presented something puzzling, rarely seen, or that included the researcher in action. However, we found very few. title: The Impact of Terrorism on Indian Tourism
abstract: Abstract This research article provides an in-depth, multi-dimensional examination of the complex relationship between terrorism and the tourism industry in India. Tourism serves as a foundational pillar of the Indian economy, contributing substantially to Gross Domestic Product (GDP), employment generation, and socio-economic development across diverse regions. However, the industry is inherently sensitive to perceptions of safety, stability, and geopolitical security. This paper investigates the immediate and long-term economic and psychological impacts of terrorist incidents on international tourist arrivals (ITA), domestic travel patterns, and revenue streams. By synthesizing historical data, analyzing pivotal case studies such as the 2008 Mumbai attacks, evaluating the nuances of modern "digital diplomacy," and examining the role of domestic tourism as a shock absorber, this study explores the systemic resilience of the Indian tourism sector. The findings suggest that while terrorism triggers significant short-term volatility and creates complex "spillover effects" on global risk perception, the Indian market exhibits high systemic resilience. This resilience is fundamentally driven by a robust domestic tourism base, proactive crisis management, and an evolving framework of "resilient branding." This paper ultimately argues that the future of Indian tourism depends on the sophisticated integration of advanced digital risk management, public-private partnerships (PPP), and a strategic move toward experiential and decentralized tourism models that decouple physical security incidents from destination perception. We further posit that true resilience requires shifting from a reactive posture—where policies are formed in the wake of trauma—to a proactive, integrated security-hospitality model that treats traveler safety as a core component of the "Incredible India" value proposition. This analysis aims to serve as a roadmap for stakeholders in managing the delicate balance between openness and security in an era of asymmetric threats. Keywords: Terrorism, Indian Tourism, Economic Impact, Security Perception, Crisis Management, Resilience, Tourism Policy, Destination Image, Soft Power, Digital Diplomacy, Risk Mitigation, Economic Multiplier, Experiential Tourism 1. Introduction The tourism industry is frequently categorized as a "peace-time industry," a designation that underscores the fundamental requirement of free, safe, and frictionless movement of people across borders. For a developing nation like India, which boasts immense cultural, historical, and geographical diversity—ranging from the high-altitude landscapes of the Himalayas to the tropical backwaters of Kerala—tourism is not merely an economic activity but a vital engine for national development and a primary instrument of soft power. It fosters infrastructure growth, provides direct and indirect employment to millions of individuals, and preserves diverse cultural heritages that might otherwise vanish in the face of rapid urbanization. Since the liberalization of the Indian economy in the early 1990s, the sector has grown exponentially, becoming a beacon for foreign investment and a cornerstone of the "Incredible India" brand, which has successfully marketed the country’s ancient heritage to a global audience. However, India has historically navigated a complex landscape of regional security and asymmetric threats, making it an ideal case study for examining the nexus between security and travel. This research seeks to provide a rigorous, evidence-based analysis of the causal link between terrorist activities and the tourism sector. It examines not only the immediate, observable fiscal losses but also the underlying dynamics that allow the sector to sustain itself—and eventually recover—amidst persistent, localized, and sometimes nationalized security threats. By exploring the triad of security, perception, and economics, this study aims to provide a strategic roadmap for policy makers, hospitality stakeholders, and international organizations to build a more secure, inclusive, and resilient future for Indian tourism. Beyond the immediate economic metrics, the scope of this study encompasses the social and psychological dimensions of travel security. As India seeks to position itself as a global leader in tourism, the ability to manage and mitigate the reputational damage associated with security incidents becomes a defining feature of a mature, globally competitive tourism market. This introduction sets the stage for a critical examination of how India has managed the transition from a passive, reactive posture to a sophisticated, technology-integrated, and proactive approach to tourism security. The evolution from a destination defined by its colonial history to one defined by modern dynamism necessitates a parallel evolution in how security and hospitality interact in the global public eye. The challenge is to maintain the allure of a vibrant, welcoming destination while simultaneously addressing the legitimate security concerns of international visitors, ensuring that the "Incredible India" narrative remains untarnished by the shadow of global instability. 2. Literature Review: The Theoretical Framework of Risk Academic literature on the tourism-terrorism nexus consistently highlights that the hospitality sector is among the most vulnerable to geopolitical instability. The relationship between terror and tourism is governed by several theoretical frameworks that explain how localized events translate into global industry shocks, creating a volatile environment where perception often outweighs physical reality. The Demand Side (Risk Perception Theory): Prospective international tourists, heavily influenced by global media cycles and government-issued travel advisories, often exhibit a heightened perception of risk. This leads to a rapid decline in demand for destinations associated with conflict, a phenomenon often described as the "cancellation effect." In the age of social media, this perception is amplified by the "geographic shadow" effect, where the perceived risk area extends far beyond the actual site of an incident, causing cancellations in regions that are geographically remote and objectively safe. Travelers often lack the granular geographical knowledge to distinguish between an affected urban center and a peaceful province thousands of kilometers away. This ignorance leads to a "blanket" risk assessment that disproportionately punishes unaffected regions. Cognitive biases, such as the "availability heuristic," further exacerbate this, where recent, vivid news reports override statistically objective safety data. The Supply Side (Operational Cost Inflation): Increased security requirements, higher insurance premiums for transport and hospitality, and the necessity of capital-intensive investments in surveillance technology drive up the operational costs for stakeholders. These costs squeeze profit margins, forcing providers to balance competitive pricing with elevated security standards. Often, the investment in "hard" security measures like metal detectors, perimeter walls, and X-ray scanners can create an institutionalized atmosphere of fear, which may indirectly detract from the guest experience by emphasizing the threat rather than the destination's appeal. This leads to the "securitization trap," where the effort to make a place safer makes it feel less like a leisure destination and more like a high-risk zone. The Crisis Management Lifecycle (CMLC): Modern scholarship suggests that destinations must navigate a cycle of mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery. In India, the challenge has historically been a reactive, rather than a proactive, approach. However, there is a clear shift toward "proactive resilience," where stakeholders are integrating crisis communication into their standard marketing strategies to maintain brand equity even during periods of volatility. This lifecycle approach emphasizes that recovery begins long before an incident occurs, through the building of strong stakeholder relationships, regular audits, and the establishment of transparent, real-time communication channels. It involves moving from a "crisis response" mindset to an "issue management" mindset. The Substitution Effect: Existing models suggest that international tourists rarely stop traveling entirely following a localized conflict; rather, they substitute their intended destination for one perceived as safer. The challenge for India, therefore, is to maintain its competitive position in the global tourism marketplace during periods of negative security narratives, ensuring that the "Incredible India" brand retains its allure as a preferred, rather than a risky, destination. By highlighting the unique experiences that cannot be replicated elsewhere, India seeks to raise the "cost of substitution," making the destination indispensable to the global traveler. The Social Amplification of Risk Framework (SARF): This framework explains how psychological, social, and institutional processes in the media can amplify or attenuate perceptions of risk. In the context of tourism, an incident is rarely just a physical event; it is a "communicated event." The way the media frames the event determines the longevity of the damage to the destination's image. SARF suggests that the "social station" of the victims and the "dread factor" of the attack method significantly influence the intensity of the public’s risk response, often leading to disproportionate and long-lasting avoidance behaviors. This framework is crucial for understanding why some regions struggle for years after a single incident, while others recover in months. title: The Role of Education in Shaping Social and Cultural Identity
abstract: Abstract Education serves as a foundational socialization agent, functioning simultaneously as a transmitter of cultural heritage and a critical catalyst for social evolution. This paper examines the intricate, recursive interplay between formal educational systems and the formation of both individual and collective identity. Through a comprehensive multidisciplinary analysis, it explores how curriculum design, teacher-student power dynamics, and the institutional culture of the school environment influence a learner’s perception of self, group belonging, and civic responsibility. The findings suggest that while education can foster national cohesion and cultural literacy, it frequently functions as a mechanism of exclusion for minority identities if pedagogical practices remain rigid or assimilationist. By synthesizing Social Identity Theory, Critical Pedagogy, and Bourdieu’s notions of cultural capital, this study highlights the urgent necessity for culturally responsive and pluralistic pedagogy in increasingly globalized societies. The article concludes by arguing that educational institutions must transition from engines of state-driven assimilation to platforms of pluralistic empowerment, where identity is treated as a fluid, dynamic, and multifaceted project. Keywords: Social Identity, Cultural Identity, Educational Policy, Socialization, Culturally Responsive Pedagogy, Critical Pedagogy, Inclusive Education, Bourdieu, Cultural Capital. 1. Introduction Education is rarely a neutral enterprise; it acts as both a mirror reflecting societal values and a laboratory for constructing future identities. As individuals navigate the formal pathways of schooling, they engage in a recursive process of internalizing cultural norms, linguistic registers, and social expectations. The institution of the school is, in effect, a microcosm of the state, exerting significant pressure on students to adopt specific worldviews while implicitly or sometimes explicitly others that fall outside the "ideal" citizen profile. The construction of identity within the classroom is not merely an incidental outcome of schooling; it is a foundational, if often obscured, objective of modern state-building. Historically, the advent of universal, compulsory schooling was designed to cultivate "ideal citizens"individuals who subscribe to a shared national narrative, often at the expense of regional, linguistic, or ethnic distinctiveness. This article investigates the systemic mechanisms both visible and invisible through which schools construct and constrain these identities. By examining the tension between nationalistic curricular agendas and the lived realities of increasingly diverse student populations, we can better understand how educational policy dictates the boundaries of belonging, exclusion, and democratic participation. As societies become more interconnected through digital technology and global migration, the role of education in navigating these complexities has never been more critical. We must look beyond simple academic attainment to understand how the school experience molds the architecture of the self, transforming the learner from a passive vessel into an agent of their own cultural synthesis. This study provides a deep dive into the psychological and sociological dimensions of this process, advocating for a pedagogical shift toward empowerment and plurality. 2. Theoretical Framework: The Anatomy of Identity in Education Social Identity Theory, pioneered by Henri Tajfel, posits that an individual’s sense of self is derived, in large part, from group membership. Educational environments categorize students, influencing their self-concept through two primary, interlocking vectors: The Formal Curriculum: This represents the "canon" of knowledge deemed valuable by the state. It dictates whose history is taught, whose literature is celebrated, and which scientific paradigms are validated. When this curriculum is narrow, students from non-dominant groups often perceive a painful disconnect between their home identity and the "official" identity promoted by the state, leading to a state of "double consciousness" described by W.E.B. Du Bois. This disconnect creates a cognitive barrier that can impede learning, as students must constantly mediate between the requirements of the school and the cultural authenticity of their home life. The Hidden Curriculum: Beyond the written textbooks, schools transmit values through unspoken norms, teacher expectations, and social behaviors. This "hidden curriculum" teaches students their place in the social hierarchy, reinforcing gender roles, class expectations, and ethnic prestige through the regulation of dress codes, disciplinary policies, and the physical architecture of classrooms. The subtle messages conveyed by who is praised, who is disciplined, and what is considered "proper" behavior collectively shape the student's internal map of their own social viability. Furthermore, we must integrate Pierre Bourdieu’s concept of "cultural capital." Educational systems tend to reward the cultural capital of the dominant classsuch as mastery of standard linguistic registers and familiarity with bourgeois cultural referencesplacing those from marginalized backgrounds at a distinct structural disadvantage. This necessitates an inquiry into how schools can transition from reinforcing existing inequities to dismantling them through critical pedagogy. As Paulo Freire argued, education must move away from the "banking model" of rote memorization, where students are passive vessels, toward a problem-posing methodology that validates the student’s lived experience as legitimate knowledge. By situating the classroom as a field of struggle, educators can help students decode the systemic forces that shape their identities, thereby fostering agency rather than resignation. The goal is to move toward a model of "transformative education" that views student identity as a site of potentiality rather than a deficit to be corrected. 3. The Psychology of Linguistic Displacement In many post-colonial and multicultural nations, the medium of instruction often conflicts with the learner’s home language, leading to profound identity friction. Research indicates that when schools privilege colonial or dominant languages at the expense of indigenous or heritage tongues, students frequently experience "linguistic alienation." 3.1 The Process of Alienation When a student’s primary tool for communicationtheir mother tongueis excluded from the academic environment, they are effectively told that their home culture lacks academic legitimacy. This leads to a fragmented cultural identity where the student feels compelled to perform a "school persona" that is divorced from their domestic life, often resulting in lower academic self-esteem and cultural estrangement. The school, in this scenario, functions as a site of symbolic violence, where the student's background is not merely ignored but actively invalidated. This alienation is compounded by the psychological toll of being forced to choose between linguistic assimilation and academic success, a choice that fundamentally fractures the self-concept. 3.2 Case Study: The Kura Kaupapa Māori Experience The success of bilingual integration is exemplified by initiatives such as the Kura Kaupapa Māori in New Zealand. By teaching through the medium of the indigenous language and embedding traditional Māori cultural practices into the daily curriculum, these schools demonstrate significant benefits in student outcomes. Research confirms that preserving heritage language is essential not just for cultural survival, but for stable psychological development. These programs illustrate that allowing the "home voice" to coexist with the "school voice" creates a bridge, enabling students to traverse multiple cultural worlds with confidence rather than conflict. By centering Te Aho Matua (the foundational philosophy of these schools), educators have successfully demonstrated that cultural grounding is a prerequisite for, not an obstacle to, academic achievement. This model provides a blueprint for global efforts to reclaim linguistic sovereignty within the classroom. 4. Discussion: Navigating the Globalized Challenge The contemporary challenge for educators is to balance the need for a shared national identityoften required for civic cohesion with the necessity of preserving diverse cultural backgrounds. Globalization has introduced new dimensions to this debate; students now navigate hybrid identities in a digital landscape that is both local and transnational. Additive Bilingualism: Policies that encourage proficiency in both the national/global language and the mother tongue yield the most stable identity outcomes. This prevents the "subtractive" effect where academic gain comes at the cost of cultural loss. Representational Narratives: Historical curricula must move beyond "single stories." title: Dr Payyalore Krishna Iyer Rajagopalan 1930-2024: “PKR”, the king is no more
abstract: In the 1980s, the Haffkine Institute, Mumbai, India (founded in January 1899 by Dr Waldemar Haffkine) was organising a conference and we were there at the Institute’s Director’s chamber in Mumbai. The Director of EVRC (Enterovirus Research Centre) entered and said, “There is a king called Rajagopalan. Is he here?”. Dr Rajagopalan stood up with a smile and they both shook hands. Two stalwarts of the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Prof V. Ramalingaswamy and Prof A.S. Paintal, both Padma Vibhushan awardees, were fondly calling Dr Rajagopalan as “Raja”. However, my association with him dates back to early 1983 or even earlier. Dr Payyalore Krishna Iyer Rajagopalan, 93, popularly known as “PKR”, passed away on April 29, 2024, at his residence in Chennai, India, after a brief illness. This loss has profoundly saddened the scientific community; especially the ICMR scientists. PKR’s departure came as a great shock and a deep wound, as it is gravely felt by the fellows associated with him and countless others who loved and respected him deeply in his wide network of community. Dr Rajagopalan was born on October 27, 1930, in Mukteshwar, Kumaon, Himachal Pradesh, where his father was working as a veterinarian at the Imperial Bacteriological Laboratory at the Imperial (now Indian) Veterinary Research Institute. At the age of five he was sent for school education to his maternal grandfather’s home at Tattamangalam in Palakkad district of Kerala. Later, he joined Banaras Hindu University at the age of about 15 years where he earned an M.Sc. in zoology with an entomology special paper in 1951. Professional excellence The National Institute of Virology in Pune (formerly Virus Research Centre (VRC), renamed in 1978) came into existence in 1952 as a joint venture of ICMR and Rockefeller Foundation, as a part of a global programme of investigations on arboviruses. In May 1952 PKR started his research career at VRC, and later worked as the Deputy Director of the WHO-ICMR’s Collaborative Research Unit on Genetic Control of Mosquitoes (GCMU), New Delhi in 1970 until 1975. Earlier, PKR did his MPH from University of California School of Public Health, Berkeley, USA and a Ph.D. from Poona University, India. Dr Rajagopalan had the unique opportunity to be trained by Drs William C. Reeves, Salim Ali, among other veterans. He studied dengue, Japanese encephalitis, ticks and mites, Western Equine encephalitis, bird migration, and yellow fever; in Bangkok, Japan, USA, and Germany. In addition, he spent time at the British Museum to understand mosquito taxonomy. ICMR established the Vector Control Research Centre (VCRC) at Puducherry and he was appointed as the Director of this new institute where he continued until his retirement in 1990. He led the institute for 15 years imparting high-quality leadership, strong technical guidance, and establishing well-equipped laboratories. He pioneered a five-year project on integrated control of lymphatic filariasis (LF) and generated high quality data considering that Puducherry was highly endemic to LF at that time. The results of this project provided ample opportunities to develop the LF elimination programme, a disease that was never thought to be eliminated till the early 1990s. Dr Rajagopalan continued to work on vector-borne diseases which are known to be climate-sensitive and the environment plays an important role in their biology. PKR understood this extremely well and thus, he always had an ecological approach, which gave him grand success. His significant contributions to Kyasanur Forest Disease, Japanese encephalitis, lymphatic filariasis, and malaria, will be referred by scientists for many years to come. He started M.Sc (Medical Entomology), the first of its kind in India, at VCRC. PKR is widely recognised as an untiring scientist who believed in locality-specific vector and disease management and demonstrated it well. Dr Rajagopalan retired from ICMR-VCRC on October 30, 1990. Recognitions Dr Rajagopalan received several recognitions including the Om Prakash Bhasin Award for Science & Technology in Health Sciences in 1985. Charles University, Prague, decorated him with a gold medal for his longstanding contributions to science in 1988 and Britain’s Society of Biology elected him as a fellow in 1989. He was honoured with Lifetime achievement awards by the National Academy of Vector Borne Diseases, the Association of Medical Microbiologists of India and the Parasitology Congress. Above all, he was conferred with the prestigious Padma Shree in Medicine by the Government of India in 1990. During his directorship, PKR served as a member of various scientific and technical advisory committees of WHO. Dr Rajagopalan lost his wife Leela Rajagopalan in December 2023. He is survived by his two sons and a daughter. PKR considered his colleagues as his family members. His life, though not bound by personal relations to many, was rich with memories and deeprooted relationships that shaped his legacy. This obituary cannot fully encapsulate PKR’s life, but it serves as a tribute to a person who was greatly respected. His life story is a vivid picture of dedication and service. Indeed, Dr Rajagopalan lived like a king at heart and in actions.
