title: Integrating Generations for Comprehensive Health Promotion: A Holistic Approach
abstract: Introduction Population ageing is a global phenomenon, and India is no exception, experiencing its significant demographic shift towards an increasingly aged population.[1] Increasing longevity and falling fertility have been identified as the key components of this transition.[2] Population ageing can be regarded as one of the greatest triumphs. However, it also presents challenges across various dimensions of society, including social, economic and healthcare realms.[3] Furthermore, the disintegration of the joint family system is on the rise, leaving older people without a support system.[3] Drastic changes in the social structure in the last few decades minimised the bonding between generations. Lack of companionship and communication among older adults living alone often predisposes them to various mental health issues. On the other end of the spectrum, our country also harbours nearly 9.8 million adolescents’ population, aged between 13 and 17 years, who are suffering from an array of mental disorders and require active intervention.[4] Further, the boom in social media and gaming platforms limited in-person interaction among the younger population, as a substantial portion of leisure time is invested in personal entertainment. Hence, connecting these two generations may prove beneficial as the association would be a win-win situation for both stakeholders. Intergenerational engagement involves community participation which provides an opportunity to engage older adults and younger people in a way that is mutually beneficial. Through intergenerational engagement, older adults impart their skills, experience and knowledge to the younger generation through volunteering at school and community-based activities. The experience and life lessons make the older people role models for the younger generation, leading to mutual understanding and better-connected societies. Further, the younger generation imparts moral values and lessons from real-life experiences. Intergenerational engagement is the need of the hour in propagating health promotion activities. Intergenerational Models Numerous tested and proven methods of intergenerational engagement platforms have been reported globally. Intergenerational engagement programmes often involve bringing members of different age groups together in a platform to perform pre-designed and scheduled activities that benefit both generations. This article aims to highlight some of the models that could be adopted in Indian settings. The research on productivity through intergenerational sympathy program model The Research on Productivity through Intergenerational Sympathy (REPRINTS)[5] programme was launched in 2004 in Japan. The programme aimed to foster intergenerational engagement through a picture book reading programme. Older adults aged 60 years and above were recruited into the intervention group of the REPRINTS programme and underwent intensive training for 3 months duration. The training covered various domains such as the selection of books, reading techniques and basic knowledge about the school life of the children. Subsequently, they participated in group activities including playing a hand game and bi-weekly picture book reading sessions to kindergarten students, for 18 months. Post-intervention assessment revealed that the REPRINTS model not only enhanced the physical and psychological functioning of older adults but also resulted in the healthy upbringing of children. Experience corps programme Experience Corps (ECs) Programme[6] in the United States of America involved the training and placement of volunteers aged 60 years and older in participating elementary schools for an academic year during which they assisted the teachers. The impact of The ECs™ in comparison with the non-EC schools was evaluated at the level of the individual child as well as at the school level. Prior to their involvement with EC, volunteers underwent rigorous training on various domains through lectures, discussions, exercises, role plays and handouts designed to equip them with the necessary skills. Upon placement of the volunteers in the schools, the school principal provided them with additional training or refresher training as indicated. Volunteers also received a stipend and reimbursement for out-of-pocket expenses. Timebank model To assist the elderly who live alone, a Time Bank scheme was introduced in Switzerland. In this innovative concept, the volunteers could accumulate service hours into their social security system accounts for assisting needy elderly individuals. When these volunteers themselves get old and require assistance, they are allowed to utilise the time bank to receive care from assigned volunteers. Following Switzerland, the United Kingdom has implemented a similar model. Motivated by this novel concept, Madhya Pradesh established the first time bank in India, and as of right now, the department has over 50,000 volunteers registered. Based in Jaipur, Time Bank of India Trust is a non-governmental organisation. It is the first Time Bank in India devoted to helping the country’s senior citizens.[7] At home programme The ‘At Home’ programme,[8] a collaborative initiative between the Ministry for Social Equality and the Student Union in Israel, aimed to reduce loneliness among older adults (women 62+ and men 67+) living alone. Students received subsidised accommodations in exchange for engaging in social activities such as shared meals, leisurely walks or engaging in computer studies with the older adult for at least 5 h weekly, accumulating a total of 160 h annually. Students stayed for 9–12 months, spending at least three nights per week at the residence. Older adults in the program were not entitled to ask students to do anything other than social activities such as nursing, cleaning or shopping. Tellegacy programme Tellegacy[9] was an intergenerational programme carried out in the United States that fostered community service learning experiences among university students. The programme implemented a tailored curriculum to alleviate social isolation and loneliness in older adults and to promote their health and well-being. In the Tellegacy Programme, university students referred to as Legacy Builders, were connected once a week with older adults, aged 65 years and above, known as Legacy Holders through in-person, telephonic or virtual interaction. Legacy builders had to undergo online training sessions to impart the fundamentals of goal setting, mindfulness, reminiscence therapy and practicing dialogue with an older adult, before participating in the Tellegacy Programme. Intergenerational programmes in Taiwan project The Intergenerational programmes in Taiwan (IGP-T) project[10] was aimed at improving the physical and mental health of older adults aged 60 years and above through engaging them with college students. The intervening group of older adults received IGP-T activities for 90 min once a week for 8 weeks while the control group received general health services. Post-intervention assessment suggested an improvement in the physical health status and emotional well-being of older adults among the intervention group as compared to the control group. Intergenerational live-in students programme Lai et al. (2022)[11] in Australia explored the effect of ongoing inter-generational live-in student program (ILiSP) which facilitated contact between older adults in residential aged-care facilities and allied health students to study the effect of such interactions on meaningful engagement among older adults. The study revealed that the ILiSP provided opportunities for students to connect with older people residing in care facilities. Qualitative data also yielded themes such as interdependence, meaningful engagement and kinship associated with intergenerational contact as part of established ongoing relationships. Intergenerational Engagement through Virtual Platform While a virtual platform cannot fully replace in-person interaction, intergenerational engagement through virtual platforms has been shown to be beneficial, as documented by numerous researchers across the globe. The need for virtual interaction intensified during the COVID pandemic as the world faced strict public health measures to contain the spread of the virus. Despite its positive effects, these stringent public health measures led to social isolation, anxiety, loneliness and other mental health issues among older adults. To combat this situation, engaging older people with the younger generation via digital platforms has been tried and tested by researchers. According to Chatterjee and Yatnatti,[12] engaging with young people is a great method to keep older persons engaged over the phone and via videoconferencing while staying at home during the COVID-19 pandemic. One of the strategies to keep older people engaged would be to educate them on how to use digital platforms, by the youth. The virtual intergenerational programme conducted by Kennedy-Behr et al.[13] in Adelaide, South Australia, consisted of a 45-min session held once a week for 5 weeks. The participants in this study were children, aged 3–5 years, from childcare centres and older adults, aged 77–94 years, residing in aged care centres. The interaction between children and older people was conducted through Zoom cloud meetings, under the supervision of their respective care providers. To overcome the minimisation of intergenerational connections through virtual platforms, the investigators incorporated a sharing component to the plan to facilitate individual interactions, knowledge sharing and relationship development. Indian perspectives-The way forward Having a rich experience of customs, rituals and wisdom passed down through generations, older adults are respected and revered in the Indian context. Thus, intergenerational engagement, in India, would serve as a cornerstone of social and familial solidarity. It would play a pivotal role in the transmission of experiences, knowledge and moral and cultural values to the younger generation while imparting a sense of acceptance and belongingness to the older people, which in turn would foster their mental well-being. The interaction could be possible through multiple ways such as storytelling sessions, interactive discussions or any other innovative programs, prioritising the socio-cultural adaptability, safety and security of both generations. The Intergenerational Learning Centre (IGLC) concept,[14] the first of its kind in India, not only aimed to create opportunities for older people (grant mentors) aged 60 years and above to support underprivileged school children in their studies but also to purposefully engage the grand mentors in achieving healthy ageing. The qualitative study revealed that IGLC helped the grand mentors lead happier and more meaningful lives, while the students benefited by showing improvement in their reading, writing and speaking abilities.[14] The concept of co-living between orphanages and old age homes would serve as a unique approach to addressing the needs of vulnerable populations across the generations in a meaningful manner. The co-living facility could be a place where the residents in the orphanages would benefit from the love, care, guidance and emotional, and experiential learning of abandoned older people while the latter could derive emotional support, physical exercise (in the form of playing) and a feeling of love and respect. Through such facilities, the older culture of joint families could be practiced and worked upon to provide maximum engagement between older adults and young children. By following this model, the educational, emotional and personal development of children will be accelerated while simultaneously providing the elders present there with much-needed social interaction and physical activity. This idea of co-living sprouts from the advent of intergenerational engagement in social, educational and medical contexts. Such interactions may also help lessen generational gaps and help promote mutual familial love and respect which they may otherwise lack. Co-living facilities help achieve this at a much larger level and provide a place to facilitate such a symbiosis of generations so different from each other. This symbiotic relationship not only provides a sense of belongingness and family for those who may have experienced loss or abandonment but also promotes empathy, understanding and interdependence within the broader community. By embracing the principles of compassion and solidarity, co-living initiatives between orphanages and old age homes in India exemplify the transformative power of intergenerational engagement in fostering resilience, dignity and collective well-being. With the technical advancement in the country, intergenerational digital interaction is yet another avenue for fostering meaningful engagement and mutual learning [Table 1]. Through digital platforms, such as virtual classrooms, video calls, etc., school students, under supervision, can be engaged in multiple collaborative projects, storytelling sessions or digital literacy training sessions with the community-dwelling older people or the ones who live in old age homes.Table 1: Benefits of Intergenerational Digital EngagementIntergenerational activities offer numerous advantages for older adults, in terms of their mental, physical and emotional well-being [Figure 1].[15] The long-term effect of the REPRINTS intergenerational programme reported by Sakurai et al. describes its positive impact on promoting the physical functioning and intellectual activity of the participants.[5] Similarly, it was documented by Zhong et al.[16] that intergenerational programmes with young children bring health benefits to older people across physical, mental and social domains. Multiple studies across the globe have reported on the benefits of intergenerational engagement in improving the mental health of older adults.[17] Intergenerational engagement not only provides an opportunity for them to enhance their self-image and challenge stereotypical views of old age but also opens avenues for demonstrating that they still have contributions to offer to the community and younger generations.[17-19] Further, Intergenerational programs are capable to foster community cohesion through shared activities and enhance mutual understanding and respect between different generations. Cronan et al.[20] reported that virtual intergenerational programs have a positive influence on social inclusion. It has also been documented that enhanced social cohesion, experiential knowledge exchange and improved intergenerational bonding would equip these generations to be resilient to face challenges. Closing the digital divide plays a crucial role in enabling access to a myriad of services available online. Improved access to digital platforms equips individuals to connect with essential health services,[21] educational programmes and enables social participation. The potential of intergenerational learning to develop lifelong learning programmes with Information Communication Technology to make ICT accessible to all has been reported by various researchers.[22] Further, engaging children in providing digital literacy to older people not only promotes the positive use of digital devices by the children but also ensures their time is used constructively.Figure 1: Benefits of intergenerational engagement(Box 1): Like any other opportunities, Intergenerational engagement also comes with a set of challenges. While it offers a potential platform for knowledge and skill exchange and experiential learning, factors such as intergenerational conflicts due to the difference in communication patterns and lifestyle, inadequate engagement of the participants and the inability to maintain deep and enduring relationships could pose challenges in effectively engaging both the stakeholders.Box 1: Case studiesConclusion In this era where India is in a transition phase characterised by modernisation and globalisation, nurturing and fostering these intergenerational connections may prove beneficial not only in transferring and preserving the age-old traditions and cultural heritage but also in imparting a sense of inclusion in individuals across the age group where they can live a meaningful life. Training and awareness generation about the intergenerational concept would foster empathy, social cohesion and mutual learning across age groups. Through effective intergenerational connections, our country can pave the way forward, fostering a healthy, happy and resilient population as this connecting of generations can be the catalyst for population development.Relevance to the preventive medicine: The intergenerational connections contribute to better mental health, enhanced cognitive functioning, stronger community cohesion and improved quality of life. Hence, addressing the social determinants of health is imperative for effective geriatric health promotion. For the younger generation, such engagement offers opportunities for experiential learning, the transmission of values and morals, and encouragement to adopt healthy lifestyle practices. Implications for the clinical practice: Intergenerational engagement can support medication delivery and its management, and foster empathy and values among Gen Z in a technology-driven era. The clinicians need to be aware about them.Author contribution GS: Concept, Design; manuscript editing, and manuscript review. DAK: Literature search, manuscript preparation. title: Cardiothoracic surgeon who infused basic research in Ayurveda
abstract: Quoting John Hunter’s advice to Edvard Jenner, Prof. Valiathan thought “Why think why not experiment” in the context of modernising Ayurveda sciences. He persuaded the audacious Indian Department of Science and Technology (DST) to introduce a platform called Ayurvedic Biology to develop interdisciplinary and intersectoral research in Ayurveda. This he achieved “when modern science has completely divorced from Ayurveda.” He emphasised that many observations similar to “cowpox had immunised smallpox in milkmaids” led Jenner to invent vaccination, available in Ayurveda in the past and the current time when its physicians treat thousands of patients with chronic illness. MS Valiathan called Ayurveda the “Mother of all life sciences.” He was a renowned cardiothoracic surgeon who practised, taught and saved the lives of thousands of patients when cardiac surgery was not as advanced as in 2024. Wikipedia and many Google links give details of his life, contributions to the field of cardiology and indigenously “Made in India” TTK-Chitra cardiac valve, which is a major milestone in India’s history of cardiac surgery discipline.[1] He received many accolades for these contributions in India, such as Padma Shri to Padma Vibhushan (2005) and internationally, Chevalier in the order of Palmes Académiques of French Government to Dr. Samuel P. Asper International Award from the Johns Hopkins University. He was the first batch of MBBS students from Thiruvananthapuram Medical College (1951). He had difficulty getting a job when he returned from the USA (1972). He struggled in somewhat less satisfying jobs in New Delhi and Chennai until he got an invitation from the Chief Minister of Kerala, Achyuta Menon, to set up the Sri Chitra Institute in Thiruvananthapuram. 5 years after joining as its director, it became an Institute of National Importance (INI) by an act of the Parliament. The Ayurveda fraternity in India is thankful to him for supporting, advocating, and providing guidance and funding to Ayurveda research through the premier institutions/departments he was associated with or able to persuade. Ayurveda recognizes his outstanding contributions in translating classical treatises of Ayurveda as Legacy of Caraka, Sushruta and Vagbhata. Decoding the Sanskrit language of Ayurveda science in the current context of allopathy medicine is a challenge, and he has succeeded it in these books, a rare contribution to the growth of contemporary Ayurveda, after Vaidya Bhagavan Dash, New Delhi and Prof. SA Dahanukar, Mumbai. Valiathan believed that unique scientific opportunities could arise from experimenting with Ayurveda from the perspective of contemporary science. He always expressed anguish with the modern teachings of allopathy and the learning attitudes of biomedical doctors for ignoring the history of modern medicine. He believed that India had imported the developments of modern medicine “without understanding its development.” He wrote a series of papers on the importance of traditional Indian medicine in Current Science post-retirement from his Sri Chitra Institute at Thiruvananthapuram service. He kept persuading science administrators of the country to look at the traditional Ayurveda and its benefits to the nation by reviving that science in the context of modern science. When he completed establishing the modern technology-driven and medicine-centred institute and brought it up to the laurels, he realised that “nothing in cardiac surgical practice, or indeed in modern medicine, had been contributed by an Indian.” “It disturbed me that since the advent of modern medicine in India over 200 years ago, there had been no contribution by an Indian in the causation of a disease, a drug, a surgical technique, a technology, a prophylactic regime in medicine, which had been adopted globally,” he said in an interview to Journal of Ayurveda and Integrative Medicine.[2] He says this thought has driven him to search for answers to his question, “Was there a time in India’s history when we were creative and innovative?” He found his Ayurvedic Guru in Mr. Raghavan Thirumulpad in Chalakudy, Kerala, who guided Valiathan with Ayurvedic interpretations while translating Caraka to English. Drs. Rajagopalan and Raman Kutty of Kottakkal Ayurveda Shala helped Valiathan’s journey to Sushrut and Vagbhata. His translational works became monumental in the early 21st century renaissance of Ayurveda for doctors, bureaucrats, and science managers of India who, unlike the time schooling of Valiathan, were probably not exposed to Sanskrit. When the policy-makers debated integrative medicine, Dr. Valiathan felt it would be desirable to familiarise Ayurveda with allopathy medical students in Ayurveda in a 2–3 weeks’ exposure. On the other hand, my teacher, Padma Vibhushan (2021), Cardiologist Prof. BM Hedge, takes a more aggressive view. He believes that if Ayurveda is redesigned, it can be introduced as a ‘post-graduate course for MBBS doctors’. Prof. Valiathan, during conversations with me, sometimes told me that an activist-like positioning might further expand the gap between these great sciences: Ayurveda and Allopathy. ‘Ayurveda physicians should shy away from false claims and provide data; the kind of work you have been pursuing.’ He was referring to integrative medicine treatment for lymphedema and lymphatic filariasis. His contribution to creating Ayurveda Biology within the DST is among the notable achievements of Ayurveda’s modernisation. He said, “I cannot claim that Ayurvedic Biology helps, or will help Ayurveda or Biology. Neither needs help. However, when new science and techniques are applied to old science, new sprouts of knowledge would appear.” However, he emphasized, “current frontiers and (priority) research questions should be specific to India than following leads from rich countries.” During the later years, after he became a national professor and was in the limelight of the media, he had to answer several questions that did not directly pertain to his interests, or he had anything to do with those political movements. He once said, “Caste is a shameful reality that hurt Kerala grievously. But I cannot remember caste playing a harmful role in patients.” A testimonial to the integrity of Kerala doctors in providing treatment despite the currently unfolding political movement on the ‘Indian caste census.’ Postretirement, his fascination with technology persuaded him to take up the leadership role as the executive vice president of the then Kerala State Science and Technology Council [now called Kerala State Council for Science, Technology and Environment (KSCSTE)]. He wanted to change the “unstated belief that complex technologies can only be developed by Westerners.” He believed “technology is a good servant but bad master; it should never come between doctor and patient”. Clearly, he was an empathetic doctor and believed in the healing touch of doctors, which, nowadays, is sometimes missing in busy and overcrowded modern hospitals in India. Although even contemporary India also suffers from a failure to recognise talent among young people, he probably wanted to encourage talents to be included in research through grants from the KSCSTE. He suffered from a lack of recognition when he returned from the USA after long experiences in complex but advancing areas of medicine. His mentor, Charles Hufnagel of Georgetown University, USA, said Valiathan suffered from the “India virus” and that the disease to do good for India made him return to India despite being in prestigious universities in the USA. At that time, he did not get a job at Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research (JIPMER), Pondicherry, or King Edward Memorial Hospital in Mumbai or Maulana Azad Medical College, Delhi. People whom he had written did not reply in those days. He had no regrets about such experiences in life because India’s massive heritage “monuments are testimony to the anonymity of the various sculptors and architects who built them and whose names are not recorded anywhere.” My first encounter with him was when he was in KSCSTE. I made a presentation quoting Valiathan’s papers on the need to instil research attitudes in Indian medical students and wanting funds to do clinical studies on integrative medicine. At a young age, I was unaware that Valiathan was on the committee. The proposal did not come through. While pursuing Ayurveda, I read several articles by Prof. Valiathan and Prof. Sharadini Dahanukar. Prof. Dahanukar encouraged me to do clinical studies and introduced me to Dr. Bhagavan Dash. Both were directly involved with experiments or treating patients. Translations of Ayurveda by RK Sharma and Bhagavan Dash were helpful for allopathy clinicians’ bedside learning of Ayurveda.[3] I had seen the vast personal collection of books of GV Satyavati, former director general of Indian Council for Medical Research, in her Bangalore residence and had chance to discuss with her on integrative medicine. I realised that Valiathan’s writing was similarly thought-provoking and instilled an interest in Ayurveda for someone who wanted to learn and use Ayurveda in the modern context or policy level. After the demise of Prof. Dahanukar[4] and age-related dysconnectivity with Vaidya Dash, and proximity compared to Bangalore I decided to meet Prof. Valiathan in Manipal. I requested that my dermatology teacher, the head of the department at Kasturba Medical College, Manipal, introduce me to Prof. Valiathan. He reluctantly agreed. I did not possess a laptop or pen drive then, and I had carried a tiny Power Point Presentation (PPT) and document on a floppy disc and Compact Disc (CD). I asked for a chance to share my thoughts through a PPT. He refused to let his computer be used for fear of a viral attack. He gave some suggestions and pointed out that my thoughts are elaborate, but grant making agencies are not likely to provide funding as they look unrealistic. Funding agencies may regard it as such and think that such studies are unlikely to happen in India. He advised me to build more data and later try to approach Government funding agencies. His words are true even today (2024) concerning neglected tropical diseases despite such diseases affecting the poor and large numbers in India. Sometimes later, I saw him at the Mangalore airport. I recognised him reading something while he was waiting to board the flight. I was inhibited by the thought that he may not recollect our meeting or be unwilling to discuss anything on dermatology. Using my dermatologist’s observation skills and reading body language, I walked past him a few times. I noticed that he started observing me wandering in the airport. A couple of travelers sat with for quick conversation. When he closed the book, I suddenly took courage, sat beside him, and started talking. He opened the conversation by saying, “You are from Kasaragod, an allopath interested in Ayurveda; what is your name, doctor?” We started sharing our common interest in Ayurveda. He appreciated our clinical studies on complex diseases like Lymphedema and Vitiligo using Ayurveda medicines on Ayurveda principles. We exchanged emails and continued conversation occasionally. We met at the same airport a few more times. When I went to Montpellier, he was very enthusiastic. He spent much time explaining to me about his collaborators in France. In the later years, he became familiar with our work, and he would talk about the Institute of Applied Dermatology (IAD) with a few Ayurveda enthusiasts and appreciate our data collection methods and evidence-based Ayurveda treatments. He expressed his desire to visit Kasaragod Institute (he would call IAD), but his busy schedule did not permit that. When I told him once that I consider you Dronacharya for this Ekalavya, he replied, “You are learning from my writing, but I will never ask your thumb as Guru Dakshina.” Financial support and sponsorship Nil. title: Nasutixalus jerdonii
abstract: Nasutixalus jerdonii (Günther, 1876) Figures 7, 8; Tables S 10, S 11 Synonymy and chresonymy. Polypedates jerdonii Günther, 1876: 571. Rhacophorus jerdonii — Boulenger (1882): 80; Das and Dutta (1998): 67. Rhacophorus (Rhacophorus) jerdonii — Ahl (1931): 114; Dutta (1997): 101. Rhacophorus (Rhacophorus) buergeri jerdonii — Wolf (1936): 172. Philautus (Kirtixalus) jerdonii — Dubois (1987): 73. Philautus (Philautus) jerdonii — Bossuyt and Dubois (2001): 25. Philautus sahai Sarkar & Ray, 2006: 303. Pseudophilautus sahai — Li et al. (2009): 519. Philautus sahai — Ahmed et al. (2009): 16. Raorchestes sahai — Biju et al. (2010): 1120. Frankixalus jerdonii — Biju et al. (2016): 6 –13. Nasutixalus jerdonii — Sivongxay et al. (2016): 439–440. Comments on taxonomic status. Raorchestes sahai (Fig. 7) was originally described as Philautus sahai by Sarkar and Ray (2006) based on two specimens collected by S. S. Saha on 29 February 1988 from 10 km north of Gandhigram, Changlang District, Arunachal Pradesh, India. After Biju et al. (2010), this species was placed under Raorchestes by implication (Frost 2025). Since its description, this species has not been reported from the type locality and no attempt has been made to study the types or compare them with other species in Raorchestes or other genera of small rhacophorids. We examined the type series (ZSIA 8500 and ZSIA 8501) available at the Zoological Survey of India, Kolkata. Our examination of the types revealed some characteristics that contradict the original description of the species by Sarkar and Ray (2006), such as vomerine teeth present in both types although underdeveloped (vs. vomerine teeth absent in original description) (Fig. 7); snout truncated in dorsal and lateral view, rounded in ventral view (vs. snout rounded in original description); rudimentary webbing present on hand (vs. not mentioned in original description). Thus, presence of vomerine teeth in the type specimens suggest that this species does not belong to the nominal genus Raorchestes. Between the years 2022 and 2023, we collected three rhacophorid specimens from Gandhigram that morphologically correspond to the type specimens of R. sahai based on the following set of characters such as truncated snout, protruding eyes, vomerine teeth present, tympanum distinct, rudimentary webbing present on hand, webbing well developed on foot, disc on fingers and toes, abdomen and thigh granular (Figs 7 and 8). Furthermore, in our phylogenetic analysis (ML) based on the 16 S mitochondrial gene, the newly collected samples (of both subadult and adult) formed a clade with Nasutixalus jerdonii (Günther, 1876) from northeast India (Fig. 8 A). The uncorrected p distance between the newly collected samples and available sequences of N. jerdonii from India included in this study are 0.0–0.2 % in the 16 S gene (Table S 10). We also examined the type specimens of N. jerdonii at the Natural History Museum, London collection (BMNH 1947.2.7.84 and BMNH 1947.2.7.85). Our topotypes agreed with the N. jerdonii types based on the following set of morphological characters: 1) snout rounded or almost truncate in dorsal view and nearly vertical in lateral view; 2) tympanum distinct; 3) small webbing present on hand; 4) circum-marginal groove present on finger and toe disc; 5) toe webbing moderate; 6) granular belly and ventral aspect of thigh; 7) dark patch covering posterior part of head on dorsal aspect, continuing to dorsum and posteriorly bifurcate. The following exceptions or variations were observed in the newly collected material and previously published descriptions. Biju et al. (2016) mentioned that vomerine ridges present in two oblique series without teeth. However, the original description mentioned that vomerine teeth are present. Based on our specimens collected from different parts of northeast India (Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh), most of the specimens of N. jerdonii have blunt vomerine teeth on two oblique series. In some other specimens (for example WII-ADA 3240) which is genetically similar, vomerine ridge is present without teeth. Additionally, Jiang et al. (2016) mentioned that vomerine teeth are present in N. medogensis Jiang, Wang, Yan & Che, 2016, while Yang and Chan (2018) mentioned vomerine ridge present without teeth in N. yingjiangensis Yang & Chan, 2018. Thus, this character is not consistent within the genus and species. Biju et al. (2016) mentioned that metacarpal tubercles are absent. However, metacarpal tubercles are visible in the types as well as in our newly collected specimens. Based on the morphological similarity of the topotypes to the holotype and paratype and the phylogenetically close position of the topotypes to N. jerdonii, we consider “ R. sahai ” to be a junior subjective synonym of N. jerdonii. However, none of the available DNA sequences of N. jerdonii by Biju et al. (2016) and Muansanga et al. (2022) are from the type locality in Darjeeling. Those available sequences are from the hill ranges of the southern slope of the Brahmaputra Valley. Therefore, topotypic samples are needed to determine whether N. jerdonii sensu stricto from Darjeeling and the populations from south of Brahmaputra Valley currently referred to as N. jerdonii belong to the same species or represent different species. Sarkar and Ray (2006) placed this species in the genus Philautus probably because of the small body size of the collected material. Although Sarkar and Ray (2006) referred to the type series as adults, we confirmed that the types are subadults based on the newly collected subadult and adult specimens from the type locality at Gandhigram. Additionally, this species was never compared with N. jerdonii in the past probably because both the species were placed in different genera. For taxonomic stability, we provide here an expanded description of N. jerdonii based on the newly collected material from the type locality of “ R. sahai ”. Materials examined. A subadult female (WII-ADA 1770) and an adult male (WII-ADA 1773) collected by BB, AD and NGP on 16 September 2022 at Gandhigram (27.265139°N, 96.937041°E, elevation 1120 m a. s. l.), Changlang District, Arunachal Pradesh; an adult male (WII-ADA 3240) collected from same locality by AD, SD, RNV and JDG on 23 May 2023. Description of newly collected male specimen (WII-ADA 1773; Fig. 8 B – H). Medium sized rhacophorid frog, SVL 41 mm; head slightly wider than long (HW / HL = 0.98); snout rounded in dorsal and semicircular in ventral view, vertical in lateral view; snout length smaller than eye length (SL / EL = 0.9); canthus rostralis indistinct, oblique; loreal concave; nostrils oval, laterally positioned and obliquely oriented; nostril closer to snout tip than eye; snout anteriorly depressed at internarial space; internarial space equal to inter-upper eyelid width and upper eyelid width; eyes protruding, moderate in size, less than half of head length (EL / HL = 0.42); tympanum distinct, round, nearly half of eye length (HTYD / EL = 0.47); tongue posteriorly notched; choanae round; vomerine teeth present between choanae and angular to body axis; a pair of internal vocal sac openings on lower jaw; habitus stout, its length nearly half of snout-vent length (AG / SVL = 0.47). Forelimbs slender; forearm length smaller than hand length (FAL / HAL = 0.71); third finger longest; fingers with rounded disc; disc on third and fourth finger nearly equal to tympanic diameter; circum-marginal groove present on disc; subarticular tubercles rounded and distinct; supernumerary tubercles present; palmar tubercles distinct, oval shaped; rudimentary webbing present between fingers; nuptial pad not visible. Hindlimbs comparatively stout; thigh length and tibia length equal, less than half of snout-vent length (TL / SVL = 0.43); foot length greater than thigh and tibia length (TL / FOL = 0.96); fourth toe longest; toes with rounded discs; toe discs width slightly smaller than that of fingers; circum-marginal groove present on discs; subarticular tubercles distinct and rounded; supernumerary tubercles absent; inner metatarsal tubercle present; outer metatarsal tubercle absent; webbing moderate, reaching first subarticular tubercle on fourth toe. Skin on dorsal aspect of snout and head smooth with numerous enlarged, distinct spinules including on upper eyelids; similar spinules on loreal region, below eyes, and on mandibular region; skin on dorsum smooth with numerous spinules, which decrease in number posteriorly; flank with flat granular tubercles; ventrum of head and chest smooth; abdomen granular; granules on thigh indistinct; flat tubercles below vent; forelimbs, tibia, and tarsus smooth. Colouration in life (based on specimen WII-ADA 1773; Fig. 8 F). Top and lateral sides of head brown; tip of snout with enlarged olive-brown patch to below nostrils and vertical pale yellow line at tip of snout; a similarly coloured spot in front of interorbital space; olive-brown stripe on loreal region below canthus rostralis; a similarly coloured patch below eyes, bordered with pale yellow; dark brown iris with irregular golden patches; olive-brown streak along anterior part of supratympanic fold and a few irregular spots on tympanum; dorsum pale yellowish brown with enlarged olive brown hourglass shaped patch, starting from interorbital space and covering posterior half of upper eyelids, posteriorly bifurcating in middle of dorsum, directing towards groin as gradually diffusing; two pale yellowish brown spots on dark patch, one on back of head and another elongated one on anterior part of back; flank pale brown with some irregular small olive-brown spots; dorsum of forelimb pale yellowish brown; broad olive-brown band on forearm; similar patch on base of hands and dorsal aspect of fingers; hindlimbs pale yellowish brown on top with three broad olive-brown, irregular bands on each thigh and tibia; small patch of similar colour on knees; similar bands on tarsus, base o

title: Connecting Dots…
abstract: You can’t connect the dots looking forward; you can only connect them looking backwards. So you have to trust that the dots will somehow connect in your future. – Steve Jobs A famous quote that has always resonated with me – one I only truly understood years later. Hello, let me introduce myself before we dive deeper into this quote and begin connecting the dots. I’m Pancham Cajla – a mechanical engineer turned social entrepreneur. Today, along with my co-founder and wife, Shakti Cajla, I am working towards making public spaces accessible for people with disabilities. We create Braille signage, curate sign language videos and build ramps so that individuals with visual, hearing and locomotor disabilities can move with ease and dignity. Our intent is to reduce dependence and enable equal participation in society. CHAPTER 1: SCHOOL DAYS – SCRIBE I remember when I was in Year 5 or 6. I was usually a quiet child – not particularly popular, average in studies and someone whose name teachers might not always remember. One day, while I was sitting quietly, the teacher asked as to who would like to volunteer as a scribe. Most of the class did not understand, so she rephrased the question: ‘Who would like to help a visually impaired student take his exam?’ That was the first time I learnt what a scribe was. Somehow, I immediately raised my hand in excitement, almost jumping out of my seat. I vaguely remember the teacher’s expression. She seemed a bit hesitant to pick me, as I was only average in studies and she may have preferred someone academically stronger. But seeing my enthusiasm, she smiled and said, ‘Alright, Pancham’. That weekend, I rode on my father’s scooter to the examination hall to assist the student. The examination went well, and a few days later, in the evening, our doorbell rang. It was the same visually impaired student, accompanied by his mother, carrying a box of sweets. He had passed his examination and had come to thank us personally. I believe that was the first time in my life that I truly experienced a real sense of purpose and impact. CHAPTER 2: COLLEGE DAYS – BLIND MUSIC TEACHER I come from a family of singers. My father is a great singer and an admirer of Mohammed Rafi and so is my sister. I, however, was fairly average and not particularly inclined towards music. During my college days, my father asked me to visit a colleague of his to train in classical music. Initially, I was reluctant, but I agreed out of obligation. Since he was part of the same banking society, I assumed he would be just another employee – perhaps tired after a long day. When I arrived, I was greeted by a blind man wearing thick black glasses. To see a visually impaired person living a typical life and performing daily chores in a family setup was completely new. That moment shook me and made me realise that people with disabilities can lead completely normal lives. The only difference is that the way they accomplish tasks may vary – but the outcome is just as effective. CHAPTER 3: 2010–2014 – INFOSYS, MYSORE After graduating, I secured my dream job at Infosys. The catch, however, was leaving home and relocating to the South – to the beautiful city of Mysore in Karnataka. The initial days were smooth. One day, during a team meeting, my senior mentioned forming a CSR team to carry out social initiatives and asked who would like to volunteer to lead it. No surprises – I was the first to raise my hand. My role involved organising visits and planning activities: distributing books to orphanages, visiting cancer hospitals to break the myth that cancer is non-contagious and eventually donating furniture and other amenities to a government school for the blind. Out of all these places, it was the blind school that struck a chord with me, and my visits soon became a weekly affair. Like a typical corporate professional, I worked hard during the week and looked forward to Friday nights to unwind. Yet, without fail – even with hangovers – I would visit the school early on Saturday or Sunday mornings. It became a ritual. Over time, I began connecting with the students and understanding their real challenges. I realised that the last thing they wanted was sympathy. They simply wanted to be treated equally. Importantly, they are not ‘divine’. We often carry this misconception that people with disabilities possess some sort of superpowers. In reality, they are human beings – just like everyone else [Figure 1].Figure 1: One of the activities involved playing Blind cricket on Saturday/Sunday MorningsCHAPTER 4: INDIA’S FIRST BLIND-FRIENDLY RAILWAY STATION One day, I received a call from my friend Divakar. He was almost in tears. ‘Pancham Anna, I missed my train home. Someone misled me, and I ended up waiting on the wrong platform. Why do people do this to us?’ Then, in a slightly sarcastic tone, he added, ‘You could do something more meaningful for us instead of organising music shows or treating us to pizzas over the weekend’. That hit hard. He asked me to visit their hostel that evening. I went along with a few friends to empathise with him, but what unfolded opened a Pandora’s box of challenges. Truly like an engineer, I began documenting their observations as problem statements. At the top of the list was a powerful suggestion: installing Braille signage on railings so that visually impaired passengers could identify platforms independently and board trains safely with minimal assistance. My initial reaction was dismissive: ‘That’s impossible. It’s a government entity – no one will listen. Forget installation. How about we organise a dance programme instead?’ Even as I said it, I realised how condescending it sounded. No one was impressed. Divakar remained calm and said, ‘At least convey our challenges to the railways. Is that too much to ask?’ To reassure him, I agreed – although I was convinced the meeting would go nowhere, if it even happened. A few days later, with some free time, I decided to follow through. Dressed casually, I somehow found myself at the DRM office. The attendant looked me up and down, smirked, and asked if I had an appointment or a visiting card. I had neither. He handed me a piece of paper and asked me to write my purpose. I had already decided to leave, but I wrote: ‘I wish to make Mysore Railway Station accessible for visually impaired people by installing Braille signage’. To my surprise, within five minutes, I was called in – ahead of others with appointments. Inside the large chamber, the DRM offered me tea and read my note aloud. He then asked, ‘Do we have any station in India with Braille that we can replicate?’ I replied, ‘Not to my knowledge’. He smiled and said, ‘So Mysore will be the first?’ I hesitated. ‘Sir, I don’t have a plan. I’ve only come with an idea’. He responded, ‘You’re a mechanical engineer. You’ll figure it out. Let’s set an example’. Just like that, the meeting ended. I walked out overwhelmed – excited, yet anxious about what lay ahead. That night, I couldn’t sleep. The next morning, I approached it like a final-year engineering project – breaking it down into stages, starting with research. I visited several institutions for the blind in Mysore, gathering inputs. Eventually, I found Braille signage in one college and learnt it had been sourced from an industrial area in Bengaluru, about 3–4 h away. After weeks of groundwork, I travelled to Bengaluru and visited workshop after workshop. Many turned me away, but one gentleman took interest. When I explained the purpose, he said, ‘I’ll help you. Let’s create a prototype’. I returned to Mysore, tested it with multiple students and received an overwhelmingly positive response. After 2–3 intense months, the day finally arrived. On 15th November 2015, Mysore became India’s first railway station with Braille signage. It was a proud moment – media coverage, flashing cameras and interactions with the Mysuru Member of Parliament (MP) and the District Railway Manager (DRM). For a brief moment, we felt like celebrities [Figure 2].Figure 2: L-R Pancham Cajla, Dr Lal (DRM Mysore Division) and Sh Pratap Simha (MP Mysore) on the day of Inauguration 15th November, 2015That evening, I finally relaxed and the next morning I woke up to see our work featured across newspapers. We had indeed created history. CHAPTER 5: INDIA’S FIRST BLIND-FRIENDLY RAILWAY TRAIN A week later, I packed my bags to return to Chandigarh and start something new. I bid farewell to Mysore, unaware that life had other plans. While I was still soaking in the appreciation back home, I received a call from the Mysore division. They said the DRM had another idea and asked me to return. This time, the goal was even bigger – introducing Braille signage in India’s first train of its kind, running from Mysore to Varanasi [Figure 3].Figure 3: Night before the Inauguration 25th January 2016CHAPTER 6: ADVOCACY: THE WORD SPREADS… And it happened again. Proof of concept, proof of performance and support of the community and governmental agencies. The project received appreciation from the Railway Board and led to a significant policy-level change – the inclusion of Braille signage in railway coaches so that visually impaired passengers could identify their seats independently. Looking back, it is incredible how a passion project evolved into a nationwide movement. Today, we have covered more than 180 railway stations across India. Initially supported by CSR initiatives, we now collaborate directly with the railways. Similarly, sign language integration – which we introduced in Ahmedabad in 2021 – is now part of a broader mandate for major railway stations across the country [Figure 4].Figure 4: Braille signageCHAPTER 7: FUTURE PROJECTS AND VISION When we started, our vision was simple: to see Braille signage across all railway stations in India. Today, with policy support and enhanced advocacy, that vision is steadily turning real. Our broader goal has always been to reduce dependence and enable people with disabilities to participate fully in society. We are now expanding into other public spaces – metros, hospitals, museums, schools, universities, banks and hotels. Alongside this, we conduct disability etiquette training for frontline staff to ensure more inclusive interactions. Because true inclusion is not just about infrastructure – it is about mindset. Before I close, I would like to say: it just needs one raised hand to make this world a more inclusive place for people with challenges to live in. Thank you. Feel free to connect with me at: [email protected]

title: Raorchestes kempiae
abstract: Raorchestes kempiae (Boulenger, 1919) Figures 21, 22; Tables 1, 2, S 6, S 12 Synonymy and chresonymy. Ixalus kempiae Boulenger, 1919: 208. Rhacophorus (Philautus) kempiae — Ahl (1931): 53, 69. Philautus kempiae — Bourret (1942): 450 –451; Inger (1985): 91; Ahmed et al. 2009: 16. Philautus (Philautus) kempiae — Bossuyt and Dubois (2001): 41. Raorchestes asakgrensis Naveen et al., 2024: 362, 365–370. Raorchestes kempiae — Naveen et al. (2024): 365 –367. Comments on taxonomic status. Boulenger (1919) described Raorchestes kempiae based on a single specimen collected by A. Kemp from “ above Tura ”, Garo Hills. The type locality refers to the ridge / peak immediately above Tura (see Paiva 1919). It is possible that this specimen was collected in 1917, which is evident from Paiva (1919) and Brunetti (1918) that A. Kemp was part of their expedition. However, there was no allocated voucher number available for the type in the original description. Chanda (1994) mentioned a possible location of the type specimen as the “ British Museum, (Natural History), London, U. K. ” which was followed by Bossuyt and Dubois (2001) and repeated in Frost (2025). Chanda et al. (2000) did not provide the presence of the type specimen of “ Ixalus kempiae ” or “ Philautus kempiae ” in the collection of the National Zoological Collection of Zoological Survey of India (ZSI), Kolkata (Calcutta). Recently Naveen et al. (2024) provided a photograph of a specimen in ZSI as the “ holotype ” (ZSI 18859) of R. kempiae. As there was no published literature that mentions the presence of a holotype with the voucher number “ ZSI 18859 ” prior to Naveen et al. (2024), we were unaware of this specimen during our examination of type specimens of Raorchestes / Philautus housed in ZSI. It was lost and found recently in the ZSI collections (https://zsicollections.in/specimen/ZSI0000002582). We later examined this specimen. On 27 May 2022, we encountered a few individuals of bush frogs (Fig. 21) in Tura Peak (25.502825°N; 90.23921°E; elevation 1060 m a. s. l.), West Garo Hills District of Meghalaya syntopic with R. garo but having a distinctive call pattern. These individuals resemble the original description of Boulenger (1919) by the following morphological characters: 1) dark bar on interorbital space, 2) crossbars on limbs, vertical bars on upper jaw, tubercles on dorsal surface of head and dorsum, 3) barely visible tympanum (although mentioned as “ tympanum hidden ” in original description), 4) indistinct canthus rostralis, and 5) brown marbling on throat and abdomen. Following exceptions were observed in the newly collected materials: 1) snout shape rounded or sub-oval in dorsal view (rounded in holotype), 2) nostril equidistant between eye and snout tip or closer to snout tip than eye (nostril equidistant between eye and snout tip in holotype), 3) concave stripes on dorsum diffused or not visible. For taxonomic stability, we provided an expanded description and determined the phylogenetic position based on specimens collected from the type locality. Thus, based on morphological similarity with the original description of R. kempiae, we refer to this population from “ above Tura ” as topotypic material of the species. Material examined. Holotype. ZSI 18859 (Fide: Naveen et al. (2024)), collected by A. Kemp from “ above Tura ”. Newly collected material. Topotype: three adult males (WII-ADA 1497, WII-ADA 1498 and WII-ADA 1500) collected by BB, AD and VJ on 27 May 2022 from Tura peak (25.502825°N, 90.23921°E, elevation 1060 m a. s. l.), West Garo Hills District, Meghalaya. Referred materials: two adult males (WII-ADA 1951, WII-ADA 1952) and one adult female (WII-ADA 1953) collected by BB, AD and VD on 1 July 2016 from Nongkhyllem Wildlife Sanctuary (25.90282°N, 91.80384°E, elevation 370 m a. s. l.), Ri-Bhoi District, Meghalaya; one adult male (WII-ADA 933) collected by BB and AD on 14 August 2021 from Athibung (25.541758°N, 93.626190°E, elevation 770 m a. s. l.), Peren District, Nagaland; three adult males (WII-ADA 1464 – WII-ADA 1466) collected by BB, AD and VJ on 24 May 2022 from Tura Forest IB campus (25.51596°N, 90.17733°E, elevation 230 m a. s. l.), West Garo Hills District, Meghalaya; three adult males (WII-ADA 1476 – WII-ADA 1478) and one female (WII-ADA 1480) collected by BB, AD and VJ on 24 May 2022 from Daribokgre (25.48974°N, 90.32374°E, elevation 1140 m a. s. l.), West Garo Hills District, Meghalaya. Diagnosis. Medium sized Raorchestes, SVL 17.8–22.9 mm in adult males and SVL 23.0– 23.3 mm in adult females; head width equal to or greater than length (HL / HW = 0.91–1.01); snout rounded to sub-oval in dorsal view; snout longer than inter-upper eyelid width; canthus rostralis indistinct; numerous tubercles on dorsal surface of head, dorsum, and limbs; numerous spinules on dorsum; pale brown dorsally; pair faint concave brown stripes (“) (”) on dorsum; faint crossbars on limbs; short brown streak present on groin. Redescription of holotype (ZSI 18859). Holotype is in bad condition and completely dehydrated (Fig. 21). Lower jaw broken; forelimbs broken at elbow; outer two fingers of the right hand damaged; hindlimbs broken at tibio-tarsal articulation; left foot broken at the base; except first toe, all other toes damaged. Small sized Raorchestes, SVL 16.5 mm; head slightly wider than its length (HL / HW = 0.93); snout rounded in dorsal view and lateral view; snout length equal to eye length; nostril equidistant between eye and snout tip; canthus rostralis indistinct; loreal slightly concave; eyes moderate sized (EL / HL = 0.46); internarial distance smaller than inter-upper eyelid width (IN / IUE = 0.88) and greater than upper eyelid width (UEW / IN = 0.62); tympanum and supratympanic fold invisible; vomerine teeth absent; tongue notch at posterior end; trunk nearly half of snout-vent length (AG / SVL = 0.48); tibia slightly longer than thigh (TL / TBL = 0.93); subarticular tubercles on fingers and toes distinct, rounded; inner metatarsal tubercle present; circum-marginal groove present on finger and toe disc. Skin on dorsal aspect of head and dorsum shagreened; flat tubercles visible on upper eyelid visible; skin on dorsal aspect of forelimb and hindlimb smooth; skin on throat smooth; belly and ventral side of thigh granular; tibia smooth. Dorsal aspect of head, dorsum and limbs brown; upper eyelids pale greyish brown; slightly dark broad patch below eye present; pair of slightly dark concave stripes on dorsum barely visible; a broad and very faint cross bar visible on thigh and tibia; throat, belly and ventral aspect of limbs brown, paler than dorsal colour. title: A report on the 24th Al-Bawasil International Camp for Children with Diabetes- We Can, We Can!!
abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an auto-immune condition that requires insulin and diabetes education (DE), along with some permanent changes to daily routine. DE is the heart of diabetes management. As the saying goes, “Give a man a fish and he will not go hungry that day. Teach him how to fish and he will not be hungry for the rest of his life.” In the same way, DE will enhance diabetes self-management skills, build confidence, and improve the quality of life. It is important to give the children the opportunity to learn about diabetes through parents, peers, healthcare professionals, or any other resources. Our goal for Children with Diabetes (CwD) is to make them capable of taking a greater proportion of responsibility for their diabetes. To become friends with diabetes (or at least not to see it as an enemy), as it will probably be easier to manage diabetes well. One such friendly approach to delivering DE in a playful, attractive, child-friendly manner that we came across at the end of December 2023 was at the 24th Al-Bawasil International Camp for Children with Diabetes in Qatar. Al-Bawasil means “the brave ones.” It is a 6-day disciplined program organized by the Qatar Diabetes Association (QDA) and supported by the International Diabetes Federation.[1,2] The objectives of the camp were, to teach self-management skills, to allow children to get involved with other children from different regions and build a cooperative environment amongst all of them, give them a chance to express themselves, discover their talent, build teamwork, adopt the principle of equal treatment, teach them healthy eating and importance of adopting a physically active lifestyle. This year the camp was scheduled at Aspire Academy, Doha, Qatar. It is a gigantic sports academy adorned by numerous quotes, which were enough to inspire anyone. There were eight participating countries predominantly from the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region (Jordan, Iraq, Iran, Bahrain, Kuwait, Libya, Sudan, Syria, Algeria, Tunisia, Turkey, and Qatar) with 66 CwD aged between 7 and 11 years [Figure 1]. The majority of them used insulin pumps and a few used insulin pens with continuous glucose monitors. This was the first time the camp invited countries from the Southeast Asian region namely, India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. The children from this region were on insulin pens and used glucose monitoring devices. MS was fortunate to supervise two girls with diabetes from India (Dr. Banshi Saboo, Diacare-Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India). HA supervised two girls with diabetes from Qatar.Figure 1:: Bawasil and supervisors from different countries at 24th Al Bawasil International Camp from children with diabetesAll children were divided into four groups and each group had two captains. The groups were named after wild plants found in the barren deserts of Qatar. Plants that grow and thrive in difficult climatic conditions. The significance of such naming is to show CwD that they can live in this world with diabetes, overcome their challenges, and flourish at the same time. They were, Al-Shafalah, Al-Aaqool, Al-Awsaj, and Al-Sidra (our group). Each group had its anthem (With determination and ability, give them greetings, Creative idea, give them greetings) and a common camp anthem as well. (We do not know anything impossible, We can, we can. To remain as light guiding the coming generations, We can We can.) These anthems were the soul and charm of the camp that carried positivity and motivation to overcome the challenges of diabetes. The anthem was pronounced by each group frequently and piercingly and this continued till the last day. Each group made sure they were the loudest than the other. During the entire camp, CwD were always referred to by the name Bawasil (the brave ones). The program encompassed diabetes workshops on injection techniques, insulin, nutrition, and storytelling on diabetes. In addition, it had arts and crafts activities, fashion shows, acts on sustainable living, talent shows, and sports activities. All of these activities were completed in one day of preparation and presentation. Groups were given markings and false Riyals for every activity to motivate participation and earn additional Riyals. The presentation was held every evening, and Dr. Abdulla Al Hamaq (Executive Director of QDA) was there to witness it each day. We were deeply touched by his kind gesture and his approach to CwD. Professor Adel M. El Sayed (Egypt) and Professor Sehnaz Karadeniz (Turkey) were also at the camp. From the third day till the sixth day, there were trips to the Oli Oli Doha’s Children Museum, Doha Expo 2023, Heenat Salma Farm, and Souq Waqif. (According to history vendors here used to stand and sell their goods, hence named standing market, Waqif means standing.) The camp concluded with the unforgettable closing ceremony, during which Bawasil, the supervisor, and other members wore their traditional attire and recounted their experiences—exchanged traditional gifts from their respective countries, speeches from Dr. Abdulla Al Hamaq and Professor Adel M. El Sayed. The backbone of the camp was its volunteers and supervisors, who were quite enthusiastic and proactive. They were from varied backgrounds medical students, caretakers of T1D, and a few from nonmedical backgrounds. They have been selected intensively from a large pool of people and had received T1D training beforehand. Each supervisor was assigned two CwDs, few of them met for the first time during the camp. The voluntary service did not involve any monetary gain or any other advantage. We were curious to know their reason for participation in the camp. The responses received were, “It is fun to be around children.” “It is a service to humanity.” “I was on vacation and thought to contribute to some good work.” “We cannot expect money in return to every work, the creator bless you in many different ways.” Experience as Caretakers There was a feeling of extreme anxiety related to blood glucose values, which may be due to over-concern. Children played all day, went on trips, ate less sometimes more, and took action against hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia or when they looked a bit low. All these instances and more made us apprehensive. Consequently, we gave frequent reminders to test the glucose levels. The sense of discomfort and irritation was visible on the young faces. We realized that continuous glucose monitoring is an integral tool that can help to decrease the burden of diabetes management. Moreover, frequent outings and less food intake due to differences in food choices made us suspicious of hypoglycemia. Next, being a part of a camp made us realize that we need to think of the consequences before engaging in any activity. For instance, on a trip to Heenat Salma Farm, we assumed the blood glucose might drop down as we would have to walk through the farm and the children would be playing all day long. We made sure we had enough supplies to treat hypoglycemia. In other instances, like eating specific food we assume blood glucose will shoot up. To a greater extent, these assumptions prevent us from getting into serious adverse events. Moreover, carbohydrate counting and insulin dose adjustment were the core part of the camp. The QAD Dietician Committee played an active part in helping each child and supervisor to make a healthy choice and inject insulin mindfully. However, children from India had different food choices as compared to children from the MENA region. We were worried, about what food would be there for meals, what a child prefers to eat, or whether he will be able to eat all on the plate. In addition, the insulin dose needs to be adjusted accordingly. At times it has happened that children took insulin, but did not like the food. In such a case, we insisted they eat appropriately to avoid hypoglycemia. Throughout the camp, we were able to maintain blood glucose levels within range without experiencing any severe hypoglycemic events. That brought us a sense of accomplishment. The feelings of anxiety, guilt, and fear are only the tip of the iceberg. There are many such events that parents of T1D come across in this journey. To them, diabetes is a daily battle that they are equipped to win. The camp allowed us to see the strength it takes to manage this condition daily and it is a true test of resilience and courage. Research has proved that parents collaborating with children can be an effective coping strategy for both.[3] In summary, such an educational camp increases self-confidence by establishing friendships with other CwDs who have to abide by the same rules on insulin, diet, and testing. It helps to normalize the condition and live with it. Moreover, it increases diabetes self-management skills. It is more fun to take insulin together and see what your blood glucose levels are and compare it with your fellow diabuddy. It was worth noting that giving child responsibilities away from their parents can help them to gain strength and boost their confidence. Supervising a diabetes camp is a completely different experience than delivering teachings face to face. It allows us to put our feet in others’ shoes who are involved in raising T1D kids. Although there were fears, anxiety, and worries, DE and experiences helped to manage diabetes during the camp. Acknowledgements We would like to express our special thanks to Dr. Abdulla Al Hamaq (Executive Director of QDA) and Mr. Ashraf for inviting us to the 24th Al-Bawasil Camp. I (Mahira) am sincerely grateful to Dr. Banshi Saboo for putting his trust and choosing me for this unique opportunity. We extend our gratitude to the Medical Committee and Dietician Committee for looking after us and making us comfortable. Lastly, big thanks to the Communication Committee, Activity Committee, and Control Committee for providing us with all the facilities that were required. Comments on taxonomic status. Boulenger (1919) described Raorchestes kempiae based on a single specimen collected by A. Kemp from “ above Tura ”, Garo Hills. The type locality refers to the ridge / peak immediately above Tura (see Paiva 1919). It is possible that this specimen was collected in 1917, which is evident from Paiva (1919) and Brunetti (1918) that A. Kemp was part of their expedition. However, there was no allocated voucher number available for the type in the original description. Chanda (1994) mentioned a possible location of the type specimen as the “ British Museum, (Natural History), London, U. K. ” which was followed by Bossuyt and Dubois (2001) and repeated in Frost (2025). Chanda et al. (2000) did not provide the presence of the type specimen of “ Ixalus kempiae ” or “ Philautus kempiae ” in the collection of the National Zoological Collection of Zoological Survey of India (ZSI), Kolkata (Calcutta). Recently Naveen et al. (2024) provided a photograph of a specimen in ZSI as the “ holotype ” (ZSI 18859) of R. kempiae. As there was no published literature that mentions the presence of a holotype with the voucher number “ ZSI 18859 ” prior to Naveen et al. It was lost and found recently in the ZSI collections (https://zsicollections.in/specimen/ZSI0000002582). We later examined this specimen. On 27 May 2022, we encountered a few individuals of bush frogs (Fig. 21) in Tura Peak (25.502825°N; 90.23921°E; elevation 1060 m a. s. l.), West Garo Hills District of Meghalaya syntopic with R. garo but having a distinctive call pattern. For taxonomic stability, we provided an expanded description and determined the phylogenetic position based on specimens collected from the type locality. title: Nasutixalus jerdonii
abstract: Nasutixalus jerdonii (Günther, 1876) Figures 7, 8; Tables S 10, S 11 Synonymy and chresonymy. Polypedates jerdonii Günther, 1876: 571. Rhacophorus jerdonii — Boulenger (1882): 80; Das and Dutta (1998): 67. Rhacophorus (Rhacophorus) jerdonii — Ahl (1931): 114; Dutta (1997): 101. Rhacophorus (Rhacophorus) buergeri jerdonii — Wolf (1936): 172. Philautus (Kirtixalus) jerdonii — Dubois (1987): 73. Philautus (Philautus) jerdonii — Bossuyt and Dubois (2001): 25. Philautus sahai Sarkar & Ray, 2006: 303. Pseudophilautus sahai — Li et al. (2009): 519. Philautus sahai — Ahmed et al. (2009): 16. Raorchestes sahai — Biju et al. (2010): 1120. Frankixalus jerdonii — Biju et al. (2016): 6 –13. Nasutixalus jerdonii — Sivongxay et al. (2016): 439–440. Comments on taxonomic status. Raorchestes sahai (Fig. 7) was originally described as Philautus sahai by Sarkar and Ray (2006) based on two specimens collected by S. S. Saha on 29 February 1988 from 10 km north of Gandhigram, Changlang District, Arunachal Pradesh, India. After Biju et al. (2010), this species was placed under Raorchestes by implication (Frost 2025). Since its description, this species has not been reported from the type locality and no attempt has been made to study the types or compare them with other species in Raorchestes or other genera of small rhacophorids. We examined the type series (ZSIA 8500 and ZSIA 8501) available at the Zoological Survey of India, Kolkata. Our examination of the types revealed some characteristics that contradict the original description of the species by Sarkar and Ray (2006), such as vomerine teeth present in both types although underdeveloped (vs. vomerine teeth absent in original description) (Fig. 7); snout truncated in dorsal and lateral view, rounded in ventral view (vs. snout rounded in original description); rudimentary webbing present on hand (vs. not mentioned in original description). Thus, presence of vomerine teeth in the type specimens suggest that this species does not belong to the nominal genus Raorchestes. Between the years 2022 and 2023, we collected three rhacophorid specimens from Gandhigram that morphologically correspond to the type specimens of R. sahai based on the following set of characters such as truncated snout, protruding eyes, vomerine teeth present, tympanum distinct, rudimentary webbing present on hand, webbing well developed on foot, disc on fingers and toes, abdomen and thigh granular (Figs 7 and 8). Furthermore, in our phylogenetic analysis (ML) based on the 16 S mitochondrial gene, the newly collected samples (of both subadult and adult) formed a clade with Nasutixalus jerdonii (Günther, 1876) from northeast India (Fig. 8 A). The uncorrected p distance between the newly collected samples and available sequences of N. jerdonii from India included in this study are 0.0–0.2 % in the 16 S gene (Table S 10). We also examined the type specimens of N. jerdonii at the Natural History Museum, London collection (BMNH 1947.2.7.84 and BMNH 1947.2.7.85). Our topotypes agreed with the N. jerdonii types based on the following set of morphological characters: 1) snout rounded or almost truncate in dorsal view and nearly vertical in lateral view; 2) tympanum distinct; 3) small webbing present on hand; 4) circum-marginal groove present on finger and toe disc; 5) toe webbing moderate; 6) granular belly and ventral aspect of thigh; 7) dark patch covering posterior part of head on dorsal aspect, continuing to dorsum and posteriorly bifurcate. The following exceptions or variations were observed in the newly collected material and previously published descriptions. Biju et al. (2016) mentioned that vomerine ridges present in two oblique series without teeth. However, the original description mentioned that vomerine teeth are present. Based on our specimens collected from different parts of northeast India (Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh), most of the specimens of N. jerdonii have blunt vomerine teeth on two oblique series. In some other specimens (for example WII-ADA 3240) which is genetically similar, vomerine ridge is present without teeth. Additionally, Jiang et al. (2016) mentioned that vomerine teeth are present in N. medogensis Jiang, Wang, Yan & Che, 2016, while Yang and Chan (2018) mentioned vomerine ridge present without teeth in N. yingjiangensis Yang & Chan, 2018. Thus, this character is not consistent within the genus and species. Biju et al. (2016) mentioned that metacarpal tubercles are absent. However, metacarpal tubercles are visible in the types as well as in our newly collected specimens. Based on the morphological similarity of the topotypes to the holotype and paratype and the phylogenetically close position of the topotypes to N. jerdonii, we consider “ R. sahai ” to be a junior subjective synonym of N. jerdonii. However, none of the available DNA sequences of N. jerdonii by Biju et al. (2016) and Muansanga et al. (2022) are from the type locality in Darjeeling. Those available sequences are from the hill ranges of the southern slope of the Brahmaputra Valley. Therefore, topotypic samples are needed to determine whether N. jerdonii sensu stricto from Darjeeling and the populations from south of Brahmaputra Valley currently referred to as N. jerdonii belong to the same species or represent different species. Sarkar and Ray (2006) placed this species in the genus Philautus probably because of the small body size of the collected material. Although Sarkar and Ray (2006) referred to the type series as adults, we confirmed that the types are subadults based on the newly collected subadult and adult specimens from the type locality at Gandhigram. Additionally, this species was never compared with N. jerdonii in the past probably because both the species were placed in different genera. For taxonomic stability, we provide here an expanded description of N. jerdonii based on the newly collected material from the type locality of “ R. sahai ”. Materials examined. A subadult female (WII-ADA 1770) and an adult male (WII-ADA 1773) collected by BB, AD and NGP on 16 September 2022 at Gandhigram (27.265139°N, 96.937041°E, elevation 1120 m a. s. l.), Changlang District, Arunachal Pradesh; an adult male (WII-ADA 3240) collected from same locality by AD, SD, RNV and JDG on 23 May 2023. Description of newly collected male specimen (WII-ADA 1773; Fig. 8 B – H).
