title: Padmashri Dr. K. M. Cherian: An outlier and maverick surgeon ahead of his time: A tribute by his students
abstract: “Chief,” as his trainees commonly addressed him, Dr. KM Cherian (Dr. KMC) has always been an outlier. One such act that defined him was his decision to return home despite having had an opportunity to settle in developed nations. That heralded the era of development of pediatric and congenital heart surgery in this part of the world. He took this plunge when everyone else did the opposite! His other acts of defiance of the status quo are far-sighted, such as working in a public hospital soon after his return to India, and all his well-known attempts to start pediatric heart surgery and thoracic organ transplantation. He wore so many hats in his professional career. A surgeon, entrepreneur, teacher, mentor, academician, and all of them with aplomb, most of the time. His dexterity and elegance in the technical performance of surgery, regardless of the type, are well known and legendary. He was probably one of the last Titans who graced the world of cardiac surgery who believed in surgery as an art first and science later. His mentorship was also unique. Never the typical teacher who holds one’s hands and trains each step. Not him. He always believed in encouraging everyone to develop their own style of technical performances. Yet, he was hostile and expressed his deep displeasure at the bloody, messy surgical fields, confusion, and the presence of too many hands all over the surgical field. Questioning the norm, or taking up cases when others had given up, or innovating procedures to make it simpler, distinguished him as a last court of appeal as far as corrective cardiac surgery was concerned in South Asia. DR. KM CHERIAN, AS A SURGICAL COLLEAGUE TO A CARDIOLOGIST It was a privilege to work as a young pediatric cardiologist with a demanding surgeon and his equally capable surgical team. Due to nonavailability of other imaging techniques in that era, echocardiography and cardiac catheterization/angiography were the only diagnostic tools for evaluation. While his expectation was always that the evaluation had to be precise, prompt, and flawless, he also understood the limitations, in which we worked. He always believed in people more than the machines they used to work with. It was not so infrequent to err in precise diagnosis and evaluation those days. It was the beginning of an era of echocardiography being the mainstay. I never recall a single incident when he made a big issue out of it. Most of the time, he shouldered the responsibility for those shortcomings. He performed surgery in numerous surgical workshops across India and worldwide, despite extremely limited resources, and despite the aforementioned constraints, he never complained about it. Even during the intervention procedures, having him around boosted our confidence levels as we felt secure and protected in case of any complications. Of course, we used to have big dressing down after the procedures in those times, but he always bailed us out regardless of the time. Many colleagues perceived him to be dictatorial and authoritative. But as senior cardiologists working with him, we found him the easiest surgeon to work with, a surgeon who openly accepted his errors of omission and commission. Another notable attribute was that he always encouraged interventional workshops in cath labs as another means to stretch the frontiers of medical science. This stood us in good stead during the formative period of the specialty of pediatric cardiology in India. Patients poured in from all corners of the world for his care as a last resort of hope. He always felt a moral obligation beyond the call of his duty. His candor and disarming opinions, often being self-critical during the mortality and morbidity meetings, enriched all of us, and we also found it deeply inspiring. Never one to hide, he always brought out the flaws in the system that we created and attempted to find solutions to improve the system. I wish modern-day surgeons would continue to have these traits. Many of us who finished our advanced training overseas did not have many options for joining a center of excellence when we returned. We should admit that there were no other centers that had a separate division of pediatric cardiac sciences, and we considered ourselves privileged to be appointed as his colleagues. It was an exciting era of learning from him, through him, and thanks to him. He always got the best out of us. The center has always been a hub of academic activity, in addition to being an exceptional clinical platform. At any given period, there used to be either renowned surgical/cardiology guests, often esteemed members of editorial bodies of prestigious journals, renowned surgeons, ongoing surgical/interventional and morphological workshops. The entire process of preparing patients for these workshops gave us a tremendous opportunity of learning.We had the privilege of being part of several research projects, including animal trials, bovine jugular vein conduits, biomedical sciences, and even applied mechanics with the Indian Institute of Technology Chennai. During a trial of breathing exercises after a Fontan operation, a yoga teacher was appointed in the hospital to study and evaluate traditional techniques for modern-day challenges. This was a quarter of a century ago. During many of our journeys together for workshops and conferences, he always remained an energetic and enthusiastic colleague and friend. Besides, he always tried to improvise anything and everything during our stay. Be it the sense of dressing from a medical and social point of view, etiquette in meetings, dealing with patients, especially during complications, Dr. KMC remained a role model and an inspiration. All in all, his greatest qualities were perfection, professionalism, punctuality, empathy, accountability, and most importantly, responsibility. I don’t recall anyone who in his lifetime has given so much to everyone, including those who worked with him even for a shorter time, with his all-around contributions to the development of medical science.DR. KM CHERIAN, AS A DOCTOR The chief had empathy toward his patients in truckloads. More importantly, he always felt that surgeons are the custodians of their patients and their interests. He felt committed to them regardless of the challenges. He displayed humility, empathy, and compassion for poor patients. Any infraction regarding patient care or other undesirable workplace activities was dealt with an iron hand. For most of his patients and the parents of the children he treated, he was almost like a messiah, and he always carried that sense of responsibility in mind while delivering care. DR. KM CHERIAN, AS A TEACHER Corporate medical worlds in current India emphasize optics and one-upmanship. Dr. KMC, being both an employer and employee in his organizations, never focused exclusively on these ancillary or supportive issues and rather rightfully focused more on medical excellence, and with him at the helm of affairs, it was pure medical science that triumphed over glossy optics. In that context, for puritans of medical excellence, he was master par excellence. We sincerely wish that many of us were like him. Alas, changing times and circumstances, and probably our own destinies, prevent us from reaching the pinnacle of excellence in medical leadership. His mentoring was also unique, with minimal interference in our technical performance, and a comment here and there with a breezy visit behind our work and advice. Holding himself accountable for our errors and the necessary verbal whiplashes so that imperfections are perfected during our next surgical performance. Sometimes, all he said was, “Mr. X is getting better,” and our days were made, and we would be charged to aim at the pinnacle of art. Chief was an unconventional teacher and mentor, emphasizing practical and common-Sense thinking. Operative and other responsibilities were assigned, observed, and assessed. If they were successfully discharged according to his expectations, additional responsibilities were assigned. His clinical executions of surgeries, keen interest in each and every detail of each patient in the intensive care unit (ICU) whom he had operated, succinct yet effective communication with bystanders, devotion to his work while celebrating fine moments life throwing at him, passion to achieve excellence in his leadership and sense of ownership he had toward his program have been highly inspiring to those of us who had the privilege to spend decades with him. As a teacher, he encouraged healthy, although fiery discussions and arguments among cardiologists and surgeons during the decision-making processes such as cath meetings, journal clubs, and seminars. Not even those accustomed to silence were exempt from discussing an issue if there was merit in doing so. He had the ability to pull anyone and everyone into the heat of the discussions. He always believed in the idea that discussions and debates bring clarity and depth to making clinical decisions and improve the quality of care. He nurtured and supported all efforts to the best extent possible. If necessary, he arranged the artists as well for the drawings, and one can see those illustrations in most of his publications. As a painter and artist himself, he was well aware of the strengths of illustrations in articles. Many of us still feel that we underutilize ourselves and our own potential once we leave him and that speaks so much about his ability to harness so much from others. But for him, many of our published works would not have seen the light of day. Many might argue that he was authoritarian, autocratic, unforgiving, undemocratic, brash, and some of his attempts at scientific breakthroughs were attempts that defied the existing ethical and moral guidelines. But that would be grossly unfair to measure an icon’s attempt at bettering medical science during his time with the present-day yardsticks. If at all, those attempts have made cardiac science in South Asia a shade better. DR. KM CHERIAN, AS A LEADER As a leader, he always led from the front, being accountable and truthful for his actions. Some of the rules he established, including dress codes and attendance punching systems, and his sincere efforts to rectify the incomplete medical records, have been exemplary and extraordinary, considering that he was the one conceptualizing, implementing, and auditing them. I still get goosebumps narrating an incident as I (Dr. Shiva) issued a notice to him for incomplete medical records, and he complied with the directive and had the greatness to inform me about it. He always believed in authorizing and then empowering the systems that he initiated, and did not hesitate to become a willing player for that, regardless of the position and aura he carried around him. He had great leadership qualities. Once he gave the responsibility and it was accepted by us, He expected completion of the assignment regardless of the challenges and he always succeeded in getting the job done! He had this unique quality of making people work to their talent potential and bring out the best in them. He was always one of the first to arrive at the hospital and probably the last to leave. He attended to the inpatients of the entire hospital, as all of them were his patients, in daily rounds and had a mercurial memory of the preoperative status and demographic details of each one of them. We, the attending consultants seeing our respective floors, were exhausted just to see a few children under our care, let alone seeing all the patients every 24 h. There has not been a single day when we have not marveled at his devotion, panache for clinical excellence. The present generations would find it hard to believe that he still found time to celebrate his life and his times, as well as some of the fine moments of his life, despite those work schedules, a damning indictment on our current concept of work–life balance. His work ethic was most inspiring, and this has indeed rubbed off on all his trainees in various shades, as can be witnessed by the way their services are run today. For me, the chief, as all of us fondly referred to him, was everything that we were not and what we wanted to be. It has been an absolute pleasure and our privilege to work under him, be mentored by him, and work with him. Some of us have been fortunate enough to spend decades with him. There have been moments of great anguish, sadness, frustration, and anger when he was critical of our actions/inactions. Looking back, we’re glad those moments were worth the time, considering the positive impact they had on us in the long run, both personally and professionally. THE CHIEF AS AN ADMINISTRATOR Dr. KMC had been an administrative leader for almost 2 decades before we started to work with him. He knew that doctors require professional progress as a primary prerequisite for success. He also knew that patients and their feedback were the most important criterion for success in the healthcare industry. He kept the financial sustenance of the programs as a top priority and never rested on any laurels. He always saw an opportunity in any challenge that the program threw at him. His concept of starting and encouraging separate adult and pediatric cardiac programs, homograft banks, inhaled nitric oxide therapy, Ross operations, thoracic organ transplantations, and trans-myocardial revascularizations aimed to achieve success from all angles, focusing on patients, doctors, and the institutions themselves. His commitment and tenacity to accomplish the desired objectives were incredible. Backing the right personnel, right initiatives, and sustaining them for their logical fruition are the traits of great commanders. The chief had loads of them. Closer to our own work as pediatric cardiac doctors, Dr. KMC had understood the importance of creating a center of excellence in pediatric cardiac sciences. He also had the great and vital insight into its requirements – resources, manpower, and infrastructure – and the visibility it gives to the hospital. He knew that the enormous goodwill it would generate from society would offset the modest financial returns from the program, thereby ensuring handsome and comprehensive returns to the institution. It is remarkable and to his credit that the program for pediatric cardiac sciences had exclusive 3 consultants each in pediatric cardiology and pediatric cardiac surgery in 1997, with a separate pediatric cardiac ICU! An initiative that took another 10 years to realize and implement for other centers in the country. DR. KM CHERIAN, AS A COLLEAGUE Each one of us has had the pleasure and privilege of being his dear colleague. Known for his good sense of humor and desire to celebrate his beautiful life, he always had time to discuss both professional and personal issues with us, and he did his best to facilitate better lives for all of us. As his colleagues, we had the opportunity to travel with him to numerous national and international conferences. His informal sessions with us and his attempts to make us comfortable as his associates have always been exemplary. Most of us, as current leaders, have made attempts to integrate those qualities into ourselves. He made it his responsibility to project all of us at international meets as his prodigies and as men/women with great potential and promise. We say with pride that all of us, his mentees, have benefited immensely from his benevolence in this aspect. Some of us used to exchange our books of general reading, fiction, and other aspects outside the medical field with him, and we admired him for his ability to find time and inclination to read them despite his schedule. An avid reader of diverse topics, the Chief was a great company to socialize and unwind after a grueling meeting or workday. Notwithstanding, as an employer, Taskmaster, and Leader, Dr. KMC was a close colleague and confidante to many of us. It took time to get close to him, which had to be preceded by a demonstration of excellence in your work and knowledge of medical or even in practical life sciences. He was always available to us for good counsel or help in any sphere of activity, profession, or personal matter. The learning, academic, social, and camaraderie workplace environment created by him was the reason he could hold on to most of his staff despite modest remunerations offered in those times. DR. title: Corrigendum: The impacts of landscape structure changes on urban surface temperature and heat islands formation of a growing city in southern Sri Lanka
abstract: In recent years, urbanization has intensified, emerging as a major global spatial phenomenon (Withanage N. C. et al., 2023;Withanage et al., 2024;Withanage and Jingwei, 2024). Urbanization levels can range from micro-scale administrative areas to broader geographical regions (Pannell, 2002). In 2018, 55% of the global population resided in cities, with projections indicating a rise to 68% by 2050 United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division (2019). In developing countries worldwide, migration from rural areas and urban infrastructure development continue to attract populations toward cities. Rapid growth of population is a predominant factor in the acceleration of the urbanization process in developing countries due to the functioning of the "push and pull" factors. This process leads to the growth of industrialization, transportation, and infrastructure development, as well as an increase in natural resource utilization in urban areas. This multidimensional process is reshapes socioeconomic activities and alters the spatial distribution of Green Surface (GS) and Impervious Surface (IS) (United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division, 2019). Impervious surface refers to areas with high levels of built-up coverage, typically including buildings, roads, and other infrastructure.Urban areas are frequently thought of as impervious areas that are covered by roads, buildings, and other constructed structures (Withanage N. C. et al., 2023). Rapid landscape transformations, including the conversion of green surface and agricultural land into impervious surface, have introduced various challenges. These issues span multiple scales, affecting farmland fragmentation, habitat loss, and air, water, and soil pollution, alongside the spread of vectorborne diseases and rising Land Surface Temperature (LST) (Deng et al., 2016;Ho et al., 2016;Son et al., 2017;Hou et al., 2019;Ranagalage et al., 2019). Presently, scholars have identified that impervious surface changes are compatible with variations in urban LST, and that leads to the formation of UHI (Ranagalage et al., 2019;Ranagalage et al., 2020).UHI is a significant environmental issue that adversely affects the natural environment and human health. UHI is a phenomenon that comprises high thermal temperatures in IS compared with other areas. Surface UHI and atmospheric UHI are the major categories of UHI (Environmental Protection Agency, 2008). The extensive growth of construction and the expansion of IS have contributed to the rise in LST and the intensification of the UHI effect in urban areas. The intensity of UHI has been influenced by the rising temperature between 2 and 8 °C within the IS (Silva et al., 2018). Thus, Green urban planning is an essential and effective strategy for mitigating the adverse impact of UHI since adverse impacts of UHI have been propagated in the recent past. Therefore, systematic investigations of UHI using remote sensing (RS) data and techniques, integrated with geographical information systems (GIS), have been significantly increasing.Geospatial technology allows for optimal decision-making by integrating geographical data models across spatial and temporal dimensions (Withanage et al., 2024;Jayasinghe and Withanage, 2020;Wimalasena and Withanage, 2022;Withanage W. K. et al., 2023;Wijesinghe et al., 2023;Nuwanka and Withanage, 2024;Withanage et al., 2024). RS data is very important and reliable source for examining the structural changes of IS and its effects on the UHI (Weng, 2002). Advancements in RS technology have made it possible to obtain thermal and optical data from the same sensor platforms, which is beneficial for researching temperature conditions and changes in Impervious Surface (Choe and Yom, 2020). Due to the lack of meteorological data, especially in developing countries, RS methods have become an effective and reliable source for UHI and LST assessment (Jain et al., 2020;Teferi and Abraha, 2017;Ranagalage et al., 2019;Wijesinghe et al., 2024). Satellite images with different time scales have provided an opportunity to examine the magnitude of UHI in IS. Highresolution satellite data such as National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) are highly appropriate for examining the mass-scale impacts of air temperature as well moderate-resolution satellite images such as Landsat and ASTER are also fine for the analysis of LST and UHI (Weng, 2009;Cheng et al., 2022;Priyankara et al., 2019). Nighttime light data, and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data have also been utilized in previous studies to assess urban LST and the UHI effect (Marconcini et al., 2014;Paranunzio et al., 2019).There has been a wide range of scholarly studies on the Landscape dynamics contribution of UHI incorporating RS in the recent past (Santos et al., 2017;Bokaie et al., 2019;Dissanayake et al., 2019;Fonseka et al., 2019;Ranagalage et al., 2017;Estoque et al., 2017). These studies widely focus on how Land Use/Land Cover (LULC) changes have led to the enhancement of the severity of UHI in developing countries. An analysis of Landsat images from 2011 to 2019 revealed a 1.86 C increase in LST in Narayanganj City, Bangladesh (Rishid et al., 2022). Furthermore, a significant correlation was observed between LST and the Normalized Differences Built-up Index (NDBI) (Rashid et al., 2022). LULC changes have led to the growth of LST between 6.05 C from 2007 to 2020 in Wuhan City, China due to the expansion of buildup areas (Cheng et al., 2022;Wanga et al., 2019). Using Landsat TM/ETM+/OLI-TIRS images another study was conducted in Yerevan city which was in Armenia (Tepanosyan et al., 2021). That study also pointed out that the decline of LULC caused an increase in the impact of UHI (Tepanosyan et al., 2021). Normalized Differences Vegetation Index (NDVI) and NDBI were calculated using Landsat images from 2005 to 2019 in Kolkata and found that LST had rapidly increased within the urban core due to the increase of the IS over GS (Chatterjee and Majumdar, 2022). In addition, a recent study focused on the space-borne sensor data set using the Multifractal Detrended Fluctuation Analysis (MDFA) in the Indian Himalayan foothills. That study also confirmed that the urbanization process accelerated the UHI (Kimothi et al., 2023).In the Sri Lankan context, several studies can be identified on how the urbanization process and the structural transformation of the IS affect variations of LST in cities (Ranagalage et al., 2017;Dissanayake al., 2019;Ranagalage et al., 2019). Expansion of the Colombo urban area and urban density positively impacted the LST during 1988-2016 (Fonseka et al., 2019). Landsat 7 ETM + data in 2000-2001 was utilized to identify the correlation between the LU/ LC and LST distribution pattern in Colombo and they stated that the UHI is significant in the port area (Senanayake et al., 2013;Ranagalage et al., 2017).
